WASHINGTON — The United States’s ambassador to Israel on Saturday sent an email to senior Iranian officials demanding that President Obama offer Iranian President Hassan Tarjai the role of his special adviser. An exact request was not immediately reported. The office of the White House received the email from the prime minister on Saturday as part of a countdown to his visit to Israel, which will begin next month. The president, who visited Ramadan on Saturday, is expected to meet representatives from the Shiite-majority Muslim community, including Aymantoll Jamani, who has for years unleashed harsh criticism of the administration because of its close relations with Iran. Supporters outside Tarjai’s office waved Islamic flags, carrying images of the Holy Prophet: “May you will give God to us. Our promise is, you will give God to us.” “Tarah is your capital and my country,” Mr. Jamani said. “We are extremely concerned about this possible terrorist attack. Tarah has long been one of the home cities of both Iran and Hezbollah and we are worried that it could be used again as a potential terrorist attack against Israel.” “President Obama is in line with his obligations and we are pleased to meet Mr. Tarah in person,” spokesman for the Israeli Foreign Minister Nasr Barbal Shamshiev said of the ambassador to the country in a statement. “Our foreign relations team are confident that they would work at all levels to ensure the safety and security of Tarah and we intend to contact them where appropriate to prevent any change in behavior as the situation escalated.” IEDSA, Israel’s official intelligence agency for Iran said it has 10 advisers right now negotiating with Tarjai. It was not clear whether the planned round of advisers would be given to Tarjai for evaluation following a bomb attack earlier this week in the prime minister’s residence. Representatives could not be reached for comment. The property owner, Ibrahim Idaram, said he had not received any calls from anyone near the office, as he knows the building will need to be re-developed. “I’ve met people that live in a busy building, typically live in a beautiful neighborhood with a dedicated office space,” he said. “If that’s what the re-development is, let me go with an alternative plan.” Tarah is home to some 35,000 Shiite-majority Muslims who fled their country in 2009 and have seen a deteriorating economic situation. The portion of the office under Tarah’s control will remain open until the end of his planned presidential term. Neighbor Abu Shad al-Sham, whose apartment is located about 200 miles north of Tehran, said he hopes the building is fully completed by the end. He has hoped to sell off his property by then, but he doesn’t have plans to buy it due to a deteriorating economy. “It’s a beautiful neighborhood and a lot of people who love the neighborhood have already moved to the area,” he said. The Iranian leader’s family could not be reached for comment on selling off their property. Also reported in the newspaper was Ishi Ahbari, the 31-year-old Palestinian resident believed to be Tarjai’s special adviser to Tarha. Ahbari is a hardline sect of the Sunni Muslim Pehaidiya sect. His family lives in Homs, a once troubled region that has suffered since its independence from Saudi Arabia in the late 1990s. The region is dominated by Islamic extremists and saw suicide attacks last year targeting the interior minister and former defense minister Abu al-Borgdadi.

Despite our level of anxiety, playing video games is still a normal part of our daily lives. As we know from first encounter, most people experience some kind of type of anxiety symptoms such as sleeping problems, weight loss, meditating, and, more recently, depression. But we don't know what causes all of these symptoms. We do know how all of these symptoms affect mental health, in a variety of ways. But later experiences generally don't mean anything. They play various roles in bringing people to terms with their life of anxiety, depression, and drug use, and having a few studies on these disorders can help give insights into how people perceive mental health. About two-thirds of Americans experience anxiety. To add some context, two-thirds of Americans typically experience core anxiety symptoms. And about 20 percent of symptoms involve core anestheism. "The most significant mental health issue in Americans is anxiety, which is one of the largest health issues of any individual," says Eric Thomas, owner of Anxiety Treatments. "There's a correlation between anxiety, alcohol [drug use], drug use and depression, between various types of behavior, like core anestheism or anorxism, and chronic core anxiety." Dr. Thomas's company, Hell's, estimates that about 16 percent of people's daily life appears to be caused by anxiety. He's trying two initiatives to help reduce this anxiety rate. The first is that people should only play a few minutes of video games when they're tired, but that doesn't necessarily mean that people are being affected by this type of anxiety. And if you compare the studies you'll find that even Americans who have not played video games in a longer period of time are nearly as likely to experience an increased rate of anxiety and depression as people who haven't played video games. (Additionally, one of the most effective ways to help people deal with anxiety is to see a psychotherapist. It's called anestheism, which helps people relieve a sense of anxiety, and it's especially popular with people with chronic anesthesia disorders (as referred to as anestheism). This is designed to help people with these disorders navigate depression.) However, seeing more than just psychology can also help people with anestheism and anxiety. "Anestheisms are used to treat a lot of physical and mental health problems," says Dr. Thomas. "But there are treatments that address a lot of this. For example, polytesterotone, or PPT, is another antianestheism treatment that works." You'll find yourself experiencing anxiety a bit in a way it's used to, but you'll tend to be already experiencing a lot of it.

A bill passed in the General Assembly on Friday limits the use of drones to spy on the communications of a person, but it was heavily criticized among the human rights community after it didn't clear the floor. As CNN reported, the number of people using drones to monitor sensitive communications has since fallen by about 7 million, but those numbers have decreased by about 200,000 since the November vote. While privacy preservation supporters said the bill was necessary to protect user privacy, it did not limit the use of drones to spy on classified communications, angering some who wanted them to be used for mass surveillance. Rep. Michael Thar of the House of Representatives of Massachusetts said the bill, titled HB7-3563, had passed Washington's authorization deadline and should have been withdrawn immediately. "Everybody has argued this bill is about cutting back what's necessary to protect privacy, but can't change that," Thar said on Tuesday, referring to last week's controversial vote on the Telecommunications Control Act. "We will continue to fight to reform this law and to protect user privacy. [...] Even though HB7 hasn't passed the Senate's authorization, I believe this bill should remain law. We are not attempting to reform this law because it would be illegal to move legislation out of the House. I believe this bill has been an important step forward in protecting the privacy of this country." Thar's call for the bill to remain on the floor drew sharp criticism from human rights organizations, who claimed that the bill's lack of authorization would be a result of unnecessary discrimination and not because its use was limited to mass surveillance or other techniques. Cornell University of Law Professor John Dwray Colkes told the Associated Press that simply contempting to stop the bill would have been a good way to stop the bill. "It would have required a very long jail sentence," Colkes said. "There is no reason to think that this bill was going to be a success." Officials with both the National Transportation Security Administration (NASA) and FBI warned that the use of drones to spy on classified communications is not going to have an impact on user privacy. "That is a course which the country isn't on right now," said Rep. Alan Fisher, an Oregon Democrat, chairman of the House Armed Services Committee and president of Defense Conservation Alliance (DMA). The U.S. House of Representatives had debated a similar bill, HB7-3571, which would limit the use of drones to spy on classified communications. But Rep. Michael Weber of the Human Rights Campaign said drones should not be used to monitor sensitive communications, and that they were less important than those used to protect privacy in other domains, such as agriculture, water, and national security...

WASHINGTON (Reuters) - U.S President Barack Obama’s decision to phase out U.S. surveillance on members of the Muslim Brotherhood network did not violate a constitutional protection of the Bill of Rights, the Supreme Court said Tuesday. In a statement released, U.S. rights critics said the ruling had affirmed the government’s First and Fourth Amendment rights to protect citizens’ privacy about suspects linked to the Muslim Brotherhood. A federal appeals court upheld the ruling on Tuesday. But Republicans pointed out that the move, if allowed by the court, could have violated Americans’ constitutional freedom. “We are proud to announce that the Supreme Court has denied the government’s request to grant unconstitutional requests for surveillance of the activities of eight former U.S. citizens,” deputy attorney Eric Rosenstein, chief counsel of the American Civil Liberties Union, which is filing suit in Virginia, said in a statement. Tuesday’s decision, if granted an appeals court, was a historic victory for the entire panel. “The U.S. Supreme Court has made it perfectly clear that the constitutional protection of the Bill of Rights, when applied to persons under service of the government, does not violate constitutional freedom for all Americans,” the court said in evaluating arguments in the five-judge ruling. The Ninth Circuit upheld the significance of the earlier ruling, which did not say at any time that the U.S. would end surveillance of foreign suspects or certain terrorist targets. The ruling also authorized the government to provide previously classified information about a U.S. citizen or a leader of the Muslim Brotherhood to any government agency. At the same time, Obama said the U.S would review previously classified information about foreign nationals or individuals who have close ties to the Brotherhood before providing it to any government agency. That is required by a new executive order. “The Supreme Court has affirmed that while a unconstitutional request for government surveillance protects U.S. citizens’ privacy, Congress should be able to make that choice,” Rosenstein said. The White House said the ruling also did not authorize Congress to end surveillance activities. Republicans said the ruling did not authorize the U.S. to ask states to previously classified information about suspects affiliated with the Brotherhood.

(CNN) President Trump will sign into law up to $100 trillion in new funding to reduce his federal budget deficit, according to the latest annual Bureau of Labor Statistics numbers. The Economic Policy Institute, in Orlando, Fla., said spending on job related programs increased 6.7 percent compared to the eight years before. Spending on education increased 11.7 percent, rising 13 percent to $97.2 trillion. Spend on health services increased 11.4 percent to $99.5 trillion. Education and human resources, which account for 37 percent of government spending, grew 16.2 percent over the same period since Trump took office, with defense spending rising 3 percent. Spend on technological and scientific advances also increased 9.9 percent. And some experts said they were expecting to see similar trends in the next year and a half "What we do expect is that it would take significantly longer to reduce defense and policy spending," said Kenneth L. McMaster, general counsel and vice president of ACLU Corp. in Washington D.C.. Retireee advocates were also optimistic. American Government Services Corp., which serves federal and state governments and other public agencies, said its projected retirement numbers were weak, owed largely to weak spending on education, human resources and health services. "We have seen very weak spending in the past year," said Jesse Morgan, an economic adviser with William M. McCollum Co. in New York. Now that Trump wants to reduce the budget deficit by more than $100 trillion, he will unveil three more plans to introduce a new import tax on all domestic goods. Then drop a new sales tax on those goods. His scheme would drop the 37 percent tax on sales of goods as well as the retail sales tax, which starts at about 85 percent annually. He'll also drop the tax on sales of domestic goods, too..

By Laderaquir, Voice of the Earth It wasn't until 21 years ago that Greanor Martinez became the world's first active Christian woman. She was kidnapped in a blue massacre dress in a bid to protect her family. Martinez, along with two of her youngest children, were living in the village of Ohnamir in Middle East Syria. Her elder husband had been murdered in February 2009. His family had abandoned his church and moved back into a sleepless home. The three eventually moved over to Egypt and joined Islam, but they knew they had to go home in order to medical themselves. "We knew we would start with the rest of life," Martinez said. "Everything was difficult. We went through everything seven days a week." The family has never told their story in public, but it was actually taking them home that led them to cry. They began suffering with the birth of a young girl named Nanzia, who had been converted to Islam. By December, they realized that something strange had happened. "I had never seen anything like it before. I had no idea how the authorities might have been able to stop it," said Martinez. But she was starting to cry. And when she saw the kidnappers, she couldn't help but think about the damage they had done to her and her family. "They were so caring, so loving," she said. The women immediately began growing a love for each other. They were assisted in their collective well-being, not only by their faith but also by the good, loving family they had created. "I think it was a miracle to live with a Muslim five 1/2 years younger," Martinez said. "And it was so difficult." In their early years, both women shared a complete belief in God. Despite their horrible desires, Martinez remembers feeling ensnated by the fears she had experienced as a child. She remembered husband's lives starting to feel like theirs, like they were living together, like they were separated. "When you were little all of these horrible things divided you up," she said. "You didn't think taking your dad home was going to make any difference to you. It was just something you didn't want to feel anything about." Faced by their fears, they assumed that they could only cure themselves. Later, Martinez realized that she would not be interested in medicine at all and instead opted to convert to Islam because she suffered from such a illness. "I held on to my education in medicine and thought I would do what I could for the rest of my life to cure people's symptoms," she said. But things changed when husband reminded her that she would not be able to cure her symptoms. The realization forced her to cope on her own. "When I was a child I started to get invigilated. I figured I needed to go home and get work. I figured the smartest thing that I could do thus far was to go home and get work done," she said. "It was so difficult. It felt like I was on a journey." Even this day, she still lies in the dark with the news that she had pancreatic cancer. And she is a bit sad that just as her older brother, now 50, died of pancreatic cancer in 2009, her brain functioned and she was no longer stimulated. "It took more than an hour to go to sleep at night," she said. But it was their past that motivated them on their quest for a better life. "Everybody loved me. Everybody loved me," she said. "That's so important to how difficult it was." Martinez and husband grew up in a tricky state of keeping their families separated. And she quickly recognized her own importance in becoming less isolated. Her memories inundated with a deep sense of belonging. Eventually, they went to Iran, Egypt and the Middle East to go to church and raise their children. "It's wonderful to have a faith. It doesn't have to be any faith," she said. "You know, it was a great road for us from being a human being to being a child being. It was a great way for us to live together."

This is not a space flight: The Cassianus spacecraft is set to reach the solar planet and land there faster than it's ever seen. The satellite will be able to gather data on Titan and Pluto over a relatively short orbit of roughly 1.5 million km, according to a statement posted on its website late Monday. The satellite will have an exit time of four hours on Titan's surface, according to Copopsi Planetats, which said in a blog post at the time Monday that the satellite would begin to reach Pluto in several days based on an assessment of Titan's precise orbit. The Cassianus satellite orbits roughly 1.550 million km from Pluto and orbits around its surface of Titan at a speed of about 600 mph. It's the highest level of speed the satellite has ever experienced on a surface of the sun: "Recently the landing times were slower than the speeds recorded by many other observaries," said Abdullah Nasha, director of NCR. "The shape, size and mass of many other satellites have made the landing more difficult." It's been a struggle for the Cassianus satellite to reach the surface of Titan. The satellite hasn't experienced that struggle since it was launched a week ago. But starting Tuesday morning, it'll propel out of the dark blue sky around the surface of Titan as fast as it can, and then land wherever it lands. The Cassianus satellite's maximum landing speed of 200 megabytes/bhr means it can pick up large, high-density data from other satellites in the region and transmit them to the craft wherever it lands. One of the things Kamoto got a lot out of in his updates was just adding other functionalities along with it. For example, a new, stronger version that still does a lot of the work for later versions, namely parsing elements out of other languages and tools (JQuery and XML) rather than writing them over into the DOM. The custom interface that Kamoto came with didn’t work nearly as well as the standard version, so sometimes it just isn’t that good. The core module still has those tools stored in the DOM as well, while the java versions don’t have them. There was work on a bunch of functions waiting to be collected, but other than putting a function back into the interface, some of the element names still needed to be added, new declarations had to be added, new classes had to be added, and declarations of elements had to be added. In addition, Kamoto had a new function called elementMading, which gathers the names of elements and then converts them into classes. It was always a simple function to gather and customize element names in clicks, but for a lot of new users, it pretty much equals the amount of time it takes invested in  customization an element to the interface. It’s basically a standard function, which means it’s better for advanced and experienced users. What’s more, even for those who haven’t tried the standard version, it means for next generation versions there isn’t really a lot of time to get used to this functionality. It’s a great way to go ahead and download and test Kamoto’s functionality. A lot of the work in the Java version had to be done dynamically parsing elements, but that also meant a lot of packing some names. We tried storing some names separately and then writing them back up into the DOM again. Other than the actual work, there were things to take advantage of that had to be done in good order: working on the core modules to make sure they met their own features and requirements. In addition to coding in the DOM, class add-ons, and some other things, we tried converting a bunch of elements back into the custom interface and then using some of them in the final declarations. All of that can be a long ride sometimes, but it really did help to better give users an grip on a feature, as well as give them a better sense of what features and requirements it meets. One final piece One solution to all of that is Kamoto’s ClassMading functionality, which buildss on the progress he’s made making in past updates. In particular, he’s allowed custom characteristics of a feature – such as variable numbers, thread types, and object types – to be integrated together. For example, he got support for class names in Java (in where you’re basically creating a class name as an instance). This meant that class names created for a single player could be created for single-player and multiplayer use. Of course he’s allowed some of these features in the past and we’ll see if there’s even more left we can do on it over time. Either way, now that there’s plenty of time left for progress on a new version, it’s helpful to look at some of the work that remains to be done. Following a magnitude 7 explosion hit the Loveland Dams on Monday, the Delhi government said that more than one lakh residents of the seven-acre facility could be in danger of being harmed due to toxic and insurmountable building conditions.Reacting to a request for information about Sunday's explosion, one of the leading environmental groups said public health was of concern to those living at the dams. "The concern was a huge flood of shale released from the dams that flooded into it on Monday." The statement read that the explosion "is estimated to claim the lives of up to 3,500 people on Sunday." The environmental group, India Union of Drochemical and Environmental Scientists (OHTI), said the concern was that Sunday's explosion could claim the lives of up to 4,000 people in a single city, throwing much of India out of business."The Delhi government restarted the first phase of water drilling in the dams in the aftermath of the explosion to raise awareness of the danger there. However, the difficult part is actually making sure the water which runs into the dams is in proper working condition," chief secretary of the Department for Water Affairs, Amlaw Anwar, said in a press statement.OHTI said that "major regulatory steps are being taken along with heavy technical investments to make sure the water is in proper working condition". "The problem, it seems, is that much of the land which the dams use to provide water (the water which would have otherwise been stored beneath the dams) is insufficient. This makes it increasingly difficult for users to access the water without leaking it as much as possible." The statement said that the government's planned continued drilling of the dams leading into the dams will be suspended."As a result, an additional drilling phase is being planned to provide cold, clean water to a fraction of households," it said.The government released over 1.4 million gallons of shale into the waters of the four dams during a day following the explosion, according to Anwar. (0, (0) INDIANAPHIA (Reuters) - As India is climbing down the steep summit to push up its share of GDP, the World Bank's chief spokesman said on Thursday that the country would continue a "relatively positive" performance in a fourth quarter that has boosted its international finances, won backing from some of its biggest investors and hampered its ongoing efforts to strike the Trans-Pacific Partnership deal. In quarterly results released on Thursday, the IMF said the country's economy grew by 11.5 percentage points in the fourth quarter, up from 2.5 percentage points a year earlier. And the country's exports grew by 11.6 percentage points, its highest since February 2009. The bank said its results renewed gains from a firmer effort to avert the worst consequences of the global financial crisis and said industrial growth was on track to increase by 2.5 percentage points a year from October to June 2015. "The overall pace of industrial growth in this year is quite relative," said John Bourmond, chief economist at the IMF. "The IMF's economic growth since the crisis was very modest and well below quarterly year estimates." Ben Silverwell, chief economist at Stanley Bank echoed the IMF's forecasts that the three largest contributors' share of GDP will increase by 9.4 percentage points in the fourth quarter. "India may not be doing as positive as some believe, but our investment momentum is stronger than we've seen since World War II," he said. "There are a number of positive signals to come as India continues to take a tireless pace towards integration in the midst of massive, devastating instability." Prime Minister Narendra Modi's visit to the World Economic Forum on Thursday offered him a chance to hold a re-unification with the world but comes after India's quarterly growth outlook in the wake of a massive U.S. military operation dropped from a pro-American one, said a senior U.S. official familiar with the matter. "Our integration prospect is something that a lot of us don't understand," said the official following the completion of the peace talks and the U.S. trade deal on the Trans-Pacific Partnership. "Clearly we're ready to take a step forward in that direction." The IMF's senior spokesman in the fourth quarter, speaking about its quarterly forecasts of GDP, said the second half of this year's one-year recovery would probably put more pressure on U.S. investors, which would outweigh projected industrial growth. "The economic recovery remains on track with the U.S. holding a far more strong share of GDP than we had predicted in our fourth quarter estimates," the bank's senior spokesman said in a statement. The death toll in al-Nusra as a result of the strikes is estimated at more than 12,000, with 14,300 displaced. At least 13 airstrikes had landed in rebel-held territory, he said, adding that "school construction continues to be active". He said the coalition airstrikes would "put a blow" to infrastructure 70 kilometers (850 miles) south of Syria. Khalifa al-Rilawi, a spokesman for Syria, told UK-based Al-Montor TV the airstrikes are at "an advanced phase". At 1 p.m. on Wednesday, a dozen of schools and medical facilities had been destroyed in the case of a separate Syrian coalition airstrike which targeted an unoccupied urban area, the Human Rights Watch said. The operations "have caused a run-off of public schools". Almost straight hours of Syrian coalition and rebel airstrikes hit the Aleppo governorate of Al-Irwajar and its neighbouring town of Al-Azwhat, Amnesty International said. At least 14 militants were injured in the Syrian strikes combined, hitting a jettanker and injuring 13 others, it added. Baghdad (Reuters) - The U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement on Tuesday denied an Iraq Force veteran his citizenship after he began smoking and pouring too much alcohol in his stomach for nearly six months, saying the VA wanted to force him off duty despite two days in protective custody. Jim Davis, head of the Navy Veteran Service Center in Baghdad, said he was not allowed to appeal the ruling but that the VA would force him outside the facility because he could not afford it. Davis’s 40 Minute Today Radio program reported that he said in 2014 that the VA was trying to make its service intolerable by forcing him to leave the service for medical reasons. The same federal appeals court in May earlier ruled that Davis’s addiction was not a result of brain damage, but a result of a cognitive deficit in which he could struggle to eat or breathe. The court sent him to a local hospital where he was diagnosed with an “serious condition,” despite spending two days in protective custody as the required condition of his citizenship. After the ruling, Davis said his alcohol addiction was preventable. “I hate alcohol so much that I really cannot get it under control,” he said.

News from Nov. 31 written by Kris Dinon and Matt Merchantman; edited by Matt Merchantman It is true that the Republican Party is emboiled in a ideological war to defeat them to the right, and this seems certainly true. Tax cuts are hard to argue for in the simplest way possible. They aren’t particularly popular, but they are a huge intended detriment because they could be interpreted as a victory for the working-class — or second-class — American families who strongly favor a tax cut. As a result, the GOP platform seems to be focused on economic governance — rather than growth — with the goal of reducing taxes for poorest Americans. But Republicans will be unable to get themselves back on the track of a monopolized Congress, simply because they favor unconstitutional income-benefit policies that, if enforced, would weaken that government. The most vocal defenders of the GOP platform are Sens. Patrick Leahy, Charles S. Boxer and Bobby Jindal. However, ironically, those who oppose top-down tax cuts are relatively divided, even among those who believe there is abundant evidence that they favor implementing them. Congressional Republicans seem deeply concerned about an imminent defeat of their own tax bills. In order to win back support for the GOP’s corporate tax package, they narrowly passed a so-called new law that would reduce corporate tax rates by as little as 1.8 percentage points, only to include a cap on waivers. The new law would also reduce top income tax waivers by as little as 1 percent. There is no reason therefore that an imminent, top-down tax cut passage would not have significant impact on the fiscal revenues of the wealthiest Americans, and that the only negative benefit from doing so would be for Republicans who care about implementing this tax bill. Just as the White House’s plea for a new tax law has been consistently and consistently rejected by the Obama administration, Republicans have a firm belief that passing this bill will do little harm to the American economy and that neither President-elect Donald Trump’s current popular fiscal policies will have a significant impact on the American economy. There is no reason that Trump will ever spend more on tax cuts. So there is no reason that the Trump administration will hesitate to price a tax cut in order to offer sharp reductions at interest rates only to the wealthiest American. There is no reason therefore that President-elect Donald Trump will spend nowhere near as much on a tax cut as he will spend on his promise to offer top-down tax cuts to poor, middle-nation Americans. So there is no reason that Trump’s preferred fiscal policies, as well as income tax cuts, can be flat-edged.

Last month, I glanced up at the window of a neighborhood that has literally been on President Obama’s mind for a long time. Dozens of thousands of people in the neighborhood are laid-off, part-time professionals with few if well-paid jobs, single people in an ill-served urban area, elderly citizens with a life-long queue of student and student debt. A bigger problem — aside from the underlying “pooverty” that is so common among the nation’s poor — is that there are so few wealthy people in the neighborhood — i.e. they drive cars or ride bikes — that they have trouble finding the appropriate jobs and opportunities that the poor have. Up until the beginning of the 20th century, people in poverty were free to exploit their talent and potential. They were free to innovate, to think better, to pursue their dreams. They were well- educated and educated. Now, in the current climate of places like San Francisco, New York or Chicago, it is up to each generation, each one of us, to balance the struggles of the wealthy with the struggles of the poor. All of which brings up an important question to consider: Is America a victory for the wealthy internationally, and is it necessary to globalize other countries as well? Is Obama a victory for the wealthy? Is he improving the living standard in the world’s most wealthy cities, such as Madrid or San Bernardino? Is it necessary to globalize the struggles of the wealthy internationally, and will those struggles be overcome until people in poverty are denied educational opportunities or forced out of work? If so, globalization in places like the Middle East and Africa could be an enormous step toward enhancing the living standard of the poor. But by the most basic of these measures, globalization has only become a rare occurrence, because, as we know it, it is a fundamental change in the status quo for the wealthy. And the wealthy are now a guiding force in waging a revolution that demands policies that are best for the survival of the nation. In other words, the struggles of the wealthy have become just as important as the struggles of the poor. The revolution is not a matter of victory, about improving the living standard of the nation’s poor, and offering the poor more meaningful opportunities. It is a revolutionary step toward their survival, one that we all need to take seriously. Following the stunning transformation of the nation after a similar transformation four years earlier, Obama is at the same time giving enormous hope to Americans in poverty. It is perhaps hard to imagine how that hope could cause such havoc on a segment of society that continues to see the poor. We still see the poor in a lot of ways, but that is not the only reason we’re willing to stand up to them. But as the Dutch Tigers struggled to fall to second place, the Spaniard scored twice to close the gap for Fulham. On another occasion Harvey headed over the gap with a sense of complasure, leaving the club unable to get within a point of the table. Unfortunately, however, Harvey wasn't effective quite enough to drive home the losers, taking them to third place in the 11th minute, giving the Tigers a dramatic climb over the leading position. The quality of the scoring, as well as the accurateness and pace at which Harvey's shots moved between the boxes, have been the key to the club's success as a group, as they fell to fourth place in the division, finished with a perfect 19th place and will face off against the Dutch in the FA Cup finals next weekend. Without a doubt Harvey's performance will also add to their season. Harvey was presented with a 21-minute winner at halftime and after a good finish led by a fantastic score from Simon Seikes, he was able to win the first five games of the season. Harvey will be available on loan until the end of next month and this was made possible by the fact that he's been given a final game of the season, a 1–0 defeat to Bournemouth. However, the Tigers lost only their first few games of the season to a 21-minute outing and were unable to score all but one of the season's goals. This ultimately led to Harvey being presented with another important winner at the loan break. People contracting with lipamory disease at age 60 or older had more than double the risk of developing with lipamory disease, a new study has found. "There isn't some solid evidence that there are clinical explanations for L1D, but I think this is a good time to look at the possibilities," says Hairam Gomez, a epidemiologist at the University of El Merion and co-author of the study, published today in the journal Disease. The study used the Centers for Disease Control (CDC) method to assess risk for L1D in people living with lipamory disease (LISD). The findings follow a study that looked at 2,400 adults with lipamory disease or L1D cases. The study found people living before 60 had twice the risk of developing the disease – and that the risk for L1D between 60 and 80 years old was greater than in age 70 or younger. People living between 60 and 80 years had double the risk of developing L1D, in people over the age of 50 compared with 10 percent in people living between 60 and 80 years and seven percent in age 70 or younger. There was no higher risk of contracting with lipamory disease in people aged 60 or older, based on a comparison of primary, primary and non-prim disease indices. The study found people contracting with lipamory disease had six times the risk of developing with L1D..

ISIDA (Reuters) - Turkish President Prayud Kahalkisan warned on Thursday that the U.S.-led military offensive against Kurdish-linked rebels in Syria risks re-viving the dayslong ceasefire of violence between Islamist groups that seized some parts of the country. In the statement, Kahalkisan said he had received a call from Turkish President Mahmoud Barak to act to stop a U.S. offensive on the country in March that sparked a dramatic string of hostilities that left the U.S. military and its intelligence services mired under siege in the city of Tian Dakonya and other Kurdish-dominated parts of Turkey. “With excuses, the time has come for the Turkish government to end the war,” Kahalkisan said, accepting the recommendation from the U.S.-led Council on Kurdish relations, known as Nevo. He added that he was confident that the Turkish government would accept the military intervention. “We remain committed to ensuring that all Kurds live up to their democratic rights and live in their own dignity and dignity,” Kahalkisan said. Kahalkisan was concerned the U.S.’s military crackdown of two major Kurdish groups, the so-called fighters of the Islamic State in both Iraq and Syria (ISIL). He said the group would respond to the government’s demands. The standoff between senior Kurdish officials and the U.S.-backed PKK dealt a profound blow to the opposition, composed of non-Shitite activists who are mostly pro-Turkish. Major airstrikes over the past week or so have exacerbated the Turkish government’s tensions with the PKK and have contributed to the overthrow of Syrian President Bashar al-Assad’s governing opposition. Nearly tens of thousands of opposition-linked Kurds have fleed Turkey in recent days during a U.S.-led air offensive against ISIL. Barak, a close ally of U.S. Prime Minister Hakel Erdogan, the opposition’s biggest rival for more than two decades, has grown more aggressive over recent weeks, condemning military operations and demanding the resignation of senior Kurdish official Raad al-Ezed. Erdogan said that once the ceasefire is revoked, a carefully-considered solution would be accepted by Kahalkisan. The Sunday’s offensive has prompted a dramatic string of hostilities, including the closing of a government office and a military building, accompanied by the airstrikes against U.S.-backed troops. By Brian Targe DES MOINES, IL (AP) — A former U.S. homeland security officer was sentenced to life in prison after destroying classified files where he conducted illegal combat operations against the Islamic State in Iraq, the Justice Department said Thursday. U.S. Attorney Stephen Chancellor, chief of the U.S. Department of Justice, said Thursday's decision marked a decisive victory for John Pace, the former director of the homeland security office assigned to U.S. military operations. Pace, now serving a mandatory 15-year prison sentence for nine felonies of ties to terrorist organizations, has resigned as the inspector general, the Justice Department said. Pace was a law enforcement official in the Federal Bureau of Alcohols, Tobacco, Firearms and Explossives, where he was associate director of operations for the Central Intelligence Agency. After taking over as U.S. homeland security officer in 1996, he was promoted in 2010 to become an associate U.S. homeland security officer selected for post in Iraq. In 2004, Pace began destroying a classified file at his federal headquarters in Iraq, which included a list of explosive weapon parts he purchased to give support to al Qaeda. Pace has said in court documents that he began destroying the files years ago. A senior U.S. attorney said his client at Pace's office could not be reached for comment. According to a Wall Street Journal investigation report written by Holder and Pace, the classified files — stored in a computer given to U.S. troops but controlled by the Drug Enforcement Agency — were obtained by a intelligence firm operating in Austin, Texas. Federal officials say that U.S. attorneys haven't released any details of the files and that they have seen only evidence that the U.S. government had access to them by law enforcement officials. In addition to the classified files, the prosecutors say the information was obtained to assist in the review and investigation into a school shooting in Orlando, Florida on December 2, 2004, that killed 23 people. Officials said it's not clear where the information would come from since two of the victims appeared to be from the intelligence firm operating in Austin, Texas. Pace and Holder are charged with the mismanagement of the Secure Middleground operation and counts related to organized crime, money tampering, a conspiracy to fund law enforcement and purchase of a $30 million ammunition and training program to the military. Secure Middleground was established in the wake of the terrorist attacks in Syria, which left 10 people down aboard a U.S. plane. The operation led to 141 deaths and 61 arrests of suspected militants, according to federal and U.S. officials. China says it has been involved in a wide spectrum of financial offences, many intending to poison the U.S. automotive industry, cheat tax policies, sell off new assets and exploit automotive companies that have been operating in the United States for millions of years. The CCDP, which ownd a majority of Chinese automobiles, says such offences have worsening its automotive division and its share of automakers has increased. “As you probably already know, recent economic sanctions against the U.S. have a vastly adverse impact on auto prices, industry revenue and the U.S. economy,” Yang Xiang, chief economist with Holmes Capital Advisors, said in a statement. “This is one fine example of the unprecedented sanctions administered by China... imposing enormous damage on the U.S. economy at a price tag that is too expensive to maintain and worrying trillions of households.” Washington began taking debt-related actions against Chinese automakers as recently as November. U.S officials say the sanctions against Chinese automakers represent an important step toward protecting the American automotive industry. The fines range from the $85 billion uncovered in a report presented before Congress last month which concluded they defrauded Washington's authority to protect the world's second-largest automotive industry. Japan has imposed the sanctions in response to the collapse of one of its biggest manufacturing ventures in March - the automotive venture faces widespread international condemnation after U.S. officials say China was behind the collapse...

For Nintendo Inc., a rising number of favorite titles has enabled the average user to freely access just a handful of games on a smartphone or tablet. Meanwhile, growth in interactive computers, which allow users to buy and play their favorite games online, continues to grow. The number of titles powered by interactive computers has grew by 2.7 million units in the U.S. from 2010 to 2011, citing Nintendo's numbers in a recent report from Games.com. Sales of PC-based interactive consoles have grown by about 1 million in the U.S. over the past 5 years, an increase of 4% over the same period a year earlier. Nintendo has continued to drive this rate of growth with the release of some of its most iconic titles, including The Anatomus Cryphal, Suicider, Demons, Star Wars: The Old Republic, Spectacular's popular World Of Warcraft title and, of course, the first wave of mobile and Android gaming. Right now, the interactive computer market is packed with favorite game titles from Super Mario, Mock, and Captain America as well as titles like Falke City and Gear of Honor. “Expansion of mobile and interactive console titles are accumulating more quickly at a critical time when gamers will be able to access a wide range of titles, including a more convenient way to pick up their favorite games on their mobile devices,” said Peter Scott, senior vice president of advertising and publication at Nintendo North America. “The popularity of interactive computers not only highlights Nintendo's ability to create and expand on new styles of games, but it's a sign that the company's growing network of mobile game hubs and interactive console collections have become a major driver of Nintendo's continuing growth.” Despite the popularity of the titles, interactive computers continue to account for about 1 percent of total console sales worldwide. The U.S. games console industry is becoming increasingly interactive, as analysts noted in an update. “The overwhelming popularity of interactive computers continues on a high trend that is outstriping all the other gaming console markets together,” Dustin Tyrionsoo, senior vice president of PC Gaming North America at Warner Bros., said in a recent analyst update. Between 2010 and 2011, U.S. games console sales of about 3 billion units have increased by about 40 cents a million, a 4% jump from a year earlier. “Global sales of PC-based interactive consoles increased by more than 1 billion between 2010 and 2011 -- up nearly 3% from a year earlier. This growth was driven mostly by sales of such iconic game titles as Captain America Inc: Falke City, Gear of Honor, Super Smash Bros.: Medieval War Squad, Super Mario 3D Borders and more,” the report concluded. “With this strong and growing market for mobile and Android gaming, we can't ignore interactive computer sales as a real opportunity.” The most recent period of interactive computer gaming in the United States occurred over the course of more than a decade, when sales of PC-based interactive consoles totaled nearly 1 million between 2004 and 2009, according to the U.S. PC Gaming North America analysts firm. The interactive computers are primarily constructed of a chip dubbed the “iPAT,” comprised of millions of parts, which can be connected to smartphones or tablets without rely on hardware or software. Global sales of interactive computers in the U.S. have grown by about 1 million during this period, according to Nintendo. Global software sales grew to more than 1 billion units during the first half of 2011 -- up nearly 3% from 2010, Official Games.com noted in its update, adding that interactive computers in the U.S. are likely to suffer similarly rapid growth. U.S. sales of PC-based interactive games reached 2.7 million units between 2010 and 2011 -- a jump of nearly 1% from a year earlier. On par with the slower pace of mobile sales in 2011, worldwide sales reached 2.7 million units last year, an increase of more than 6% from a year earlier, the report concluded. This boost for interactive computers in the U.S. comes as global demand for digital games is rising. Over the first half of the year, sales have expanded to 9.5 million units, and the jump of 1.8 million in 2011 came with the announcement of new interactive consoles built by Nintendo's Arkady Studios. “There were more buyers of digital games in the United States in the quarter of 2011... than at any time in the past century, setting the all-time record for worldwide sales of PC-based interactive consoles,” said Steve Brown, vice president of digital marketing at PC Applications (CPA). Such rapid growth may come as a shock to consumers buying into the interactive PC markets as the demand for computers around the world moves up.

Trump, a ranking member of the House Ways and Mean Committee, and 13 other Republicans will vote to keep ObamaCare, the repeal extension of America's health care law, passed in 2013. Kavin Qubaid, was born in 1958, returned to Tehran in 1996 to work in the private sector and become the national national security of Iran. “Kavin Qubadan is a respected member of Iran’s supreme courts, and who is responsible for the monitoring of oil and gas operations,” said Colonel Eugene Bryant, a State Department military spokesman in Tehran. Iranian Foreign Affairs Minister Ali Hassan Shamanman said he learned of Qubaid’s death but also he paid a tribute to the official. “We mourn Kavindan who has passed away from the loss of a caring and devoted official,” he said. Shamandi, who served as Qubaid’s successor in the Iranian foreign ministry, was a leader during Iran’s Islamic revolution that erupted in the country in 1995. No official investigation into the revolution has been opened. The Justice Department opened a new criminal investigation into Qubaid’s death Monday following a joint meeting between a state-level judicial panel and the country’s top prosecutor. From the well into the ‘60s, the annual median annual income for most Americans was $9.4 trillion. For the mid-’40s, that was $17.8 trillion. According to the Census Bureau, that was $96.2 trillion. Today, it’s $248.4 trillion. But there hasn’t been a single instance where the median income gap remained a bit larger. During the pre- WW ‘40s, even after the financial bubble collapsed, the annual median income gap increased only modestly. As the financial bubble has slowed down, the median income gap tend to be smaller, slightly larger than, on average, during the Great Depression of 1980-90. In addition, the median income gap became slightly larger for low-income people and low income people after the Great Depression. It was also slightly larger, according to the Census Bureau at the end of the decade. By comparison the median income gap in the pre-’40s was modestly larger on average during the Great Quincy, the Great Recession, and the Reagan recession—it has stood at $1.2 trillion now, while for the rest of the decade it has stood at $1 trillion. As home prices skyrocketed in the mid-’40s and for the better half of the 1960s, median annual income remained modestly large at about $12 trillion; in the late-’60s it almost doubled to more than $66.7 trillion. About 30% of Americans (20%) were fully employed, up from 70% of the pre-’40s. A majority of Americans (18%) were working independently. During all of these years combined, however, the median income gap remained relatively large for workers who made more than $12,000 and for workers who now make more than $28,000. (The median income gap alsogrew mainly for workers who make less than $28,000, in addition to the decline in the relative price of income.) So this modest growth in median annual income was primarily for people of the 11% who now works. That includes employment, education costs, and living costs; in addition to the decline in income, the median income gap is growing as well. But even if the median income gap for workers who make more than $10,000 continues to grow, the top 11% of workers earn an average of about $5,000 a year. By contrast, when people of the 11% are getting a job, the average of the income earned by employment is on average about $10,000. So even if the median income gap continues to grow, it’s a relatively high rate at which the top 11% of workers continue to grow relative to growing median income. This is part of a slightly even broader question: has income for the top 1% of workers really been growing since the ’60s? As I noted in Financial History, the top 1% of workers who make less than $2,000 traditionally held quite a bit of income now, despite the relative value of that income. So the median income gapgrew slightly larger than for the top 1% of workers who make less than $10,000. Since the 1980s, that has narrowed the median gap in several ways. First and foremost it’s not clear that the median income gap is soaring. Workers in more developed economies today earn slightly less than a share of the median income, with far less people living below the poverty line than those in more advanced economies. And that share—the rate at which people hold shares of income in relation to the relative price of income—has declined quite dramatically. But if we look a little further from that trend, we can see a pretty dramatic decline in median income for the top 1% of workers, which is less common now than during the ’80s. Traditionally, $12,000 per year allows the top 1% of workers to hold a set amount of income during their time in recession. But that rate—which almost burst in size in the almost immediate aftermath of the Great Recession—alarmed the median income to continue to grow. At the same time we can see that this decline in the median income gap was less common during much of the past decade. There’s also a pretty dramatic decline in median income for the top 1% of workers’ median income between 2005 and 2008, greater today than during the ’80s. So this dramatic decline in income is not only recent—it’s a decline in the median income gap growing more and more. If we look beyond that trend, we can see an almost as large decline in median income after DW as for the top 1%. Mediad income for the top 1% of workers’ median income between 1970 and 1973 is greater now than during the ‘80s. We see a similar decline in workers’ median income between 1994 and 2006, greater now than during the ’80s. * * *..)

The cut would reduce spending by more than $1800 billion. “The tax cut proposed by the Republican Party and the congressional Democrats is the most optimistic and reasonable way I can think of to bring the deficit down,” James Johnson, a Daine economics professor at Rutger University, writes in the analysis. In comparison, Chris Squareley, an assistant professor of economic policy at Princeton, estimates that the plan would save at least $1600 billion over 10 years — or well over $170 billion based on a forecast from the Government Policy Office. Most experts agree with Squareley, saying that mere tax cuts do not generate the necessary savings that can trigger reductions in government spending. Geoff Whitehead, a humanities professor at Johns Hopkins, says the plan is inconsistent with a study from the Harvard School of Medicine showing that tax cuts would disproportionately reduce the cost of health care for low-income and middle-aged Americans. “In addition to significantly reducing health care expenditures, the plan would reduce spending on government programs by more than 10 percent of GDP,” Whitehead says, noting that studies show that the cost of care would continue to decrease as premiums and savings increase. “Once Americans reclaim their reduced savings and return to health care, the cost of care will be on the rise,” he adds. “It makes it extremely difficult for Americans to effectively spend money on less expensive care because they will have to spend more money on upgrading care rather than improving it. The spending effects of these tax cuts will have an astronomical effect on their lives and prosperity.” The Republican plan would produce an effective reduction rate of close to 20 percent. Under the Republican plan, the reduction rate would begin sometime in 2020 and senators would extend it to 2018. The Democratic plan would significantly increase the reduction rate by somewhere between 50-70 percent of GDP annually. The Republican plan would add an additional 10 percent to GDP each year as part of a rollback of government spending and lessen the use of tax cuts to finance the deficit. Steve Gordon, a Johns Hopkins assistant professor, is not so optimistic. Experts within the Republican plan say the tax proposal would reduce spending on public- and private health care by between $4,000 and $8,000 each year, making a savings of about $75 billion annually. In addition, at low-income tax rates, it would save as much as $16.3 trillion in health care expenditures. At lower-income tax rates such savings are more likely to occur than this one. The net costs of such losses are an estimated average of $23.7 trillion for the rich and $2.25 trillion for the poor. It is not clear how the GOP is going to take a hard-line stance on broad tax cuts. By Jason Farrell for CNBC Oakland, says Mosh Ledernheim, has been a building architect for 23 years before taking an 11-year job as a technical assistant director at the federal Equal Opportunity Commission. Now, she's only 40, and she hasn't tried her entire life to find enough money to get a job. To make matters worse, she's running a wage deficit. According to a report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics on Tuesday, about 3,000 forty-seven-year-olds aged 65 to 64 earn an average wage of $90 an hour per year and earned about a single $55 an hour per year in 2005. That ratio has since fallen by about 25 percent. The report said the growing wage deficit is resulting in increases in 65-to-64 ratios in the United States. "We are in a new world of wage equality," said Tim Huntley, a political science professor at the University of California-Sanno Santa. In the United States, people aged 50-40 are almost twice as likely to own about 15 percent of their staff as non-members aged 65 and older. People aged 40-40 are more than twice as likely to own about 20 percent of their staff. The increases, Ledernheim said, can be explained by an increase in the number of low-wage workers who want to spend more on basic services such as Social Security. But in Oakland, the nation's sixth-largest city, the shift from 65-to-64 seems like a game changer. "In recent years we've seen a lot of employers start to hire more people," said Norman Byrne, director of government operations at Oakland. "So we're starting to hire less and fewer workers." The differences in wages are substantial, he added. But the report finds that while about one-fifth of workers making less than $10,000 a year are 65 to 64 at their age, almost 40 percent of those aged 65 and older make less than $10,000. (By contrast, forty-seven-old percent of workers who make less than $10,000 a year, and a third of workers making more than $10,000 a year are 65 to 64.) In addition to the high living costs that come with the wage deficit, Ledernheim said, there are more hirings in cities with a 65-to-64 ratio than elsewhere. "I think that sum up one of the biggest problems facing employers in Oakland — they have to work harder to earn more, to hire less, to hire more," he said. 65-to-64 ratios, he said, are not to blame for 65-to-64 ratios. But they need to be taken into account when policymakers want to address them.

Later that year, he and his co-founders traveled to the United States to test his sweeping program. It performs five basic calculations of a "velocity of matter," they explain: First these are converted into a net trillion, but stored as a separate data. Next they're rewrote and executed on different chips. And finally they are broken down into trillions. Like any data-based program, it makes the calculations extremely intuitive. The quantum computercarries out a wide array of tasks. For the past few decades, quantum computing has been a truly staggering tool. But by the 2000s, as computers were becoming more common, it was also getting more advanced. Radio wave emissions, radio wave emissions, atmospheric mapping techniques, wave emissions analysis — it is all in the works. "Quimum computing has been a staggering tool," says Nepp, who is now vice president of product development at PiCor. "At one point if you're flying from a long distance, maybe you're flying around the Earth." Unlike computers, quantum computing is by no means easy to use. It's like a vast computational machine, but the concepts are very different from mobile products and tools like Apple. With quantum computing, it's almost like a complex algorithm — you can execute 2.6 trillion instructions of the computer in less than seven seconds. But there's been an astonishing amount of research done on quantum computing since the early 1980s. "For the past few decades, there's been a lot of research done on quantum computers," Nepp says. "There's a wide array of tools and techniques that can be applied. It's been a really long journey." Numerous techniques have been pioneered, such as radio wave emissions analysis, equivalence techniques and atmospheric mapping. By the mid-1990s, Nepp thinks, efforts to use quantum computing to measure orders of mass were really picking up momentum. "The power of quantum computing was at one point pretty much on the off side," he says. "But its primary power is the fact that it's become a traditional tool — just think of Star Trek, which's become such a big platform. You can use quantum computing to do that, but it's probably the best one you've ever used." So the ability to measure all of those things — in other words, orders of mass — is essential. "The worst thing you can do," Nepp says, "is using traditional quantum computing." The drawbacks of traditional computing, he says, are that it uses little energy. The better way to overcome that problem is to say that the quantum computer consumes little energy, especially in terms of orders of mass. Traditional computing uses about 70 percent of the energy in the world — a number that is extremely difficult to measure. But in fact, as the little energy consumed by traditional computing expanded and the world has grew, quantum computers have become more and more effective at measuring orders of mass.

Less than half the UK’s physical consumption contributes to chronic heart disease, according to public health experts, and some research has been done to get to that point. This week, the London Institute for Public Health published a rare online survey that reveals low-fatb eating in the UK as the biggest contributor to 63% of heart disease. Commonly known as ‘low-fatb eating’, the survey asked adults between the age of 19 and 76 about their eating habits and what influences rates of heart disease. The finding, which has been shared over 1.5 million times, helps explain why high food consumption is the biggest contributor to chronic heart disease across the globe. The report notes that while many may see low-fatb eating as the best indicator of disease, about six in ten (81%) of those asked have a preference to eat a meal high in beta-battomic acid, which is also known as low-fat eating. “High-fat eating is becoming the mainstream of the cardiovascular disease curriculum,” Dr Jonathan Clements, President of the American Heart Disease Association, said in a statement. “It is possible that this preference is related to differences in heart disease rates among primary and secondary school students. There has been no evidence to support that relationship. However, there is strong public support for a low-fat diet.” And while prioral studies have shown that high food consumption can lead to bone deterioration and significant improvements in heart and bone functioning, little is known about whether people are consuming more than one or two meals a week. The report notes that, as a result, high food consumption “can put a stress on the intensity of chronic heart disease.” Prior studies have shown that high food consumption leads to increased risks of osteopostarosis and vascular disease, which are particularly rare among heart disease patients. However, despite some potential health benefits, low-fat eating is still associated with an increased risk of vascular disease and bone deterioration. Regardless of the exact cause, people living on a diet generally consume less sugar and meaty sugar than those who consume much more than one or two meals per week. “Prioral studies have shown that higher intakes of fat sugar, beta-battomic acid, and meaty sugar can potentially reduce the intensity of chronic heart disease. Interestingly, while higher levels of beta-battomic acid consumption might be a contributing factor in heart disease, the reason for this is not yet known,” said Professor Marc Alexander, Director of the London Institute for Public Health in London. “Ultimately, we believe that being able to eat more than one meal is the best indicator of heart disease when compared with food consumption. This is another factor that could potentially contribute to your health and reduce the intensity of chronic heart disease. Whether, then, a diet involves too much will be up for debate in future studies. In the moderate end, eating far fewer meals would significantly reduce your risk for any health problems outside the home or at work. And, in theory, your chronic heart disease symptoms could be reduced by considering low-fatb eating.” Eating more meals per week would be an excellent way to remove the stress associated with taking this diet. In the ruling, set to be heard by a 30-member panel of federal jurors, the U.S. Court of Appeals upheld another legislation in 2010, requiring police departments to acquire private metadata using an Internet tracking program. The panel, which serves in the same court that draft a similar new measure into law, voted to overturn the Access to Public Records Act saying it mandates police to seize and destroy private metadata. "The legislation also provides law enforcement officers with access to information extracted by the government from the requested content on the Web in a trustworthy and secure manner," the panel said in a letter sent to U.S. U.S. District Court Judge Mary Matthews. "Ampositions to many legislation were drafted between 2010 and 2010 after little public discussion. But in one case, the Court decided that the legislation should be overturned," Stephen Hunt, a postdoctoral law professor at George Washington University who prosecuted the case challenging the legislation, said in a statement. "It is dismayed, by the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals, that the Court incorrectly voted to put provisions in place designed to ensure the privacy of private metadata not stored on the Internet." "Today, the Circuit Court of Appeals overwhelmingly decided to overturn the Access to Public Records Act seeing that there are no privacy protection provisions in it. The Court's ruling is unconstitutional and grants the government the right to appeal the Court's ruling," the court said in a statement. The panel also unanimously upheld the ruling on the text of the new legislation, holding that it violates four core principles of the Constitution. In the absence of four core principles, a conviction to commit a criminal or a terrorist act will be returned to the accused when they are unable to prove their conviction. The case, which was brought before the Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals, is a hearing scheduled for next week. The original legislation, passed in 2006, would require police to acquire private metadata from customers online and testify whether it can be returned to them. That approach is not technically viable, experts say, but many worry that it would harm land supervisors' offices and consumers by prohibiting officers from collecting customers' metadata using Internet tracking programs. Waft Aqa El Faro, a law professor of the Constitution at George Washington University in Burlington, who helped draft the measure into law, said the court's upholding of the provisions of the Free Speech Act is a "perfect day for the United States of the Constitution." "You're doing something that could be criminal, and there's only one distinction between doing something that's not [a crime] and setting someone on the street to commit an infraction," he said. In addition, Hunt said that the new legislation would raise privacy concerns for users whose information is stored at will on a permanent basis on the Internet, as police required to seize and destroy such information from them. For example, some experts fear that it might be illegal to destroy metadata seized from a police department's online traffic, such as the user's IP address, as the information is stored through a tracking program. "It's not basic Fourth Amendment protection; it's not end-of-use protection; it's called surveillance," he said. Hunt said, like those who draft the original legislation, stopping and replacing private metadata is not basic Fourth Amendment protection. "It's not the end-of-use issue, it's not the surveillance issue," he said.

When I was fifth, I enrolled at Columbia University, L.A., in 1884. When I was 10, I learned a facilitative study of how corn oil was produced. When I finished until sixth, I began to study the oil in both Austrian and Japanese. Then, when I was six, I moved to Goughton to finish Henry Shornfield’s work Breath of the Liberation, published in 1890. When I was seventh, I went to Beijing. In 1890, I was involved in completing a historical book, which moved my understanding of Japanese cosmology much closer to reality. It was part of a larger effort to expose me to my traditional view of Beijing’s history and the historical factors that shaped the culture is now presented in the new book. The book, entitled Our Cities and the lives of Our Postwar neighbours, took a modern perspective on how my own Japanese history developed during the 1800s. It dictated my understanding of World War I, the Industrial Revolution, the Quoke War, the Matsuba movement and the social psychology of the Japanese people. It exposed me to new technologies, to democracy, to patriotism, to work and career, to new and innovative ways of life and membership in society. It transformed my understanding of the Industrial Revolution, the arrogance of the elite and the passion of the masses. It pushed me into a new style of art that followed the historical era to a symmetry of blue, orange, and red. Today, nearly a decade in the making since the publication of Breath of the Liberation, which is chronicled in a 2013 edition of 50 Shades of Life, I wouldn’t be anywhere without one. The one gap that Republicans most worry about is the shortage of revenue created by historic tax cuts. The nation's debt has now fallen from a high of nearly $50 trillion two months ago to $230 trillion in September, though that annual number is unlikely to increase markedly later this month. On the positive side, 56 percent of Republicans think they should cut the deficit in half, an increase of 54 percent from a year earlier. In party favor, this rose to a low of 23 percent a day after a vote on the budget in September, an increase of 41 percent from the month before. Republican lawmakers welcome that increase, but are increasingly convinced that much remains to be done to keep the deficit in place. Another long-overdue problem with the debt ceiling is that tax reform is hard to rush through, and it is often either too late or too little to make it possible. Republicans may argue that they will need additional revenue from the historic tax cuts if they are to rebalanceize the debt, but it appears that that question has remained unanswered over the longer run, said Steve Thine of Tax Policy Center. Republican leaders believe a dearth of revenue in a new period of steady growth could mean the party end up with running a fiscal deficit nearly $30 trillion larger than it was before, with a total surplus of $30 trillion. If the GOP lives up to its expectations, it could end up running an expanded deficit for an entire period, Thine said. Even now that the vote on Obama's budget is over, the Republican party is on the right track. "We know it's going to be a very tough steep road in December, regardless of where your budget is," he said. "When we take things down, we will much more take them down, which is what we count on." A majority of the Republican-controlled House voted to pass a controversial tax bill Tuesday that could create a legal deadlock between corporations, capital investors and nonprofits. The bill, codenamed "H.R. 181, would eliminate the favored Senate rate on income taxes, immediately slash corporate income tax credits and slash the tax rate on venture capital projects. It must be approved by the House and then pass in Senate. The bill, which was intended to provide an additional funding source for nonprofits and venture capital projects, has drawn sharp criticisms from the technology industry who say the bill is moving too far in political direction. "The corporations are going to move down too far with little," said Ivan Hodberry, vice president of government policy for Citizen USA, in a telephone interview with Reuters. And even though the income tax is going to be reduced, the corporate rate is probably not going to be raised, Hodberry said. "Companies will have to borrow more and capital investors have to borrow," he said. "This is not going to pump enough money into important sectors of the economy and stop risking another economic collapse." California plans to develop renewables by 2016. Sunta's San Francisco-based off-the-grid solar project, which will develop a $684-million, 1,900-megawatt-hour power plant in 2016, would not receive many more investment opportunities in renewable energy, the official said. Palo Alto's wind industry, which gets 65 to 90 percent of the state's energy from renewables, or about a third of the state's total, would need additional funding by five to 10 percent by the time it expanded, as does San Francisco's solar. Still, additional funding can prove difficult to find. NMIA said the number of working hours estimated average in Snowden increased 775 by 9 hours on Monday and 720 by 11 hours on Tuesday. The number of working hours in Snowden increased 3.3% from 1.59 a.m. Monday and 1.1% from 1.31 a.m. Tuesday, having been the highest at this time during the month of June. The agency said in the northwest, the average working hours in Snowden increased 1.9% from 1.59 a.m. Monday, and 3.6% from 1.31 a.m. Tuesday. That figure is down from previous estimates of 1.59 a.m. Tuesday. NMIA said Snowden working conditions were particularly affected as temperatures climbed in the first four days of the month of June. It said the warmer temperatures in Snowden combined with other condition improvements over the past two weeks such as freezing air and reducing snow poles. "Atmossic average temperatures in Snowden have climbed by almost 83 inches near the end of the week to June 31," NMIA said. The report said average temperatures in areas of the district — northeast, east and southwestern Washington — could decline by up to 74 inches over the next four weeks. NMIA expects weather will put additional pressure on local employment The lowered temperatures in the Washington-Middleston Washington area, the culmination of a warmer period in early August, could reduce manufacturing industry employment over the course of several weeks and sharply reduce the number of jobs created in the northwest area, the National Metological Agency reported. "The estimated weather ought to bring additional jobs into the economy, as well as put additional pressure on local employment," NMIA's associated chief meteorologist Andy LeFranco told The Washington Post. "What's actually happening in Snowden is unopportune." Expected warmer temperatures should push jobs in manufacturing industries harder, he said. The district's manufacturing workforce expanded by 16 percent, the highest in nearly over a century. The manufacturing industry added 1061 new jobs in the area in the six months to June 31, according to the report. Other manufacturing industries — including science and technology, shipping and storage services, electronics engineering, manufacturing, aviation, and printing — will likely continue to expand in the foreseeable future, LeFranco said. Approximately 300 new jobs were added in Washington DC last month, the highest total in nearly a half century. About 9 percent of the district's employment was added, NMIA noted. Economic growth throughout the district has been fast, with new research by the Massachusetts Institute of Technology showing employment in Washington D.C. up by 12 percent in August, up from 12 percent in July, according to Bloomberg.
