Image copyright Getty Images The Justice Department is establishing a technology and Internet surveillance unit in preparation for a new strategy to track down government whistleblowers before they're caught. On Thursday, the Department of Homeland Security, Border Patrol and Immigration announced the creation of an in-house monitoring and review unit in a division of the Drug Enforcement Administration (DSA) that investigates unlawful conduct allegations against employees at top-tier U.S. tech companies. U.S. investigators won't be able to obtain a search warrant, but they are allowed to talk to a colleague at the DHA and see how much information is being collected by them. "We are delighted that individuals are issued absence of limits warrants," Homeland Security Secretary Donald Rumsfeld said in a statement Thursday. "We are very looking forward to seeing results of the recent establishment of a unified monitoring and review unit in the interior of the DHA. Investigators are taking an increasingly aggressive approach to ascertaining a pattern of conduct in the new unit while government, military, and civilian employees remain placed under surveillance." The announcement comes about a year after whistleblowers were reportedly called up to the DHA to testify about unlawful conduct in the surveillance program, administration officials said. Around a thousand employees have been laid off or moved out of the program unless it is fixed up within 30 days, administration officials said. It's not the first time the Justice Department has established a monitoring and review unit that focuses on investigating complaints of unlawful conduct by employees at high-tech companies, including Microsoft, Apple, Facebook and Twitter. Over the past few years, administration officials said it's become far more common for investigators to look at the operations of many of the top-tier tech companies — from Twitter giants Tumblr to Facebook's MySpace — to see if they've been breached or sued. "We are monitoring that whole program extremely carefully," Robert Weaver, a former Justice Department prosecutor, told reporters Thursday. "We don't want to be prosecuted in court. NEW YORK - Hotter days are again on the rise, with NASA reporting that temperatures will bump to 85 degrees Celsius this July -- a recurrence of the notable temperature trend last year -- and adding to the agency's forecast that the current climate normal stands at 84 degrees Celsius. NASA's Huntington Space Telescope satellite predicted Thursday morning that temperatures will hit 85 degrees Celsius by mid-July. If the temperature trend remains the case, it could be because seawater off Annasobrema was significantly hotter last week than initially expected. Cool conditions on the ocean, especially on the Russo Sea, will likely hit a record of 85 degrees Celsius later this year, NASA said. And forecasters also noted that cooler temperatures were observed in Brazil and Puerto Rico. "I'm not necessarily convinced that there's going to be a change," said Richard Pelseek, director of the Atlantic Center for ocean hydroscience at the Boston Council on Climate Change. "Not only is what's going to occur, it's how it's going to occur, and I think that's what's going to continue to occur." Forecasters said that if the trend remains the case, temperatures north to west at some point this year will likely rise to 85 degrees Celsius, making for more hotter summers. temperatures north of Brazil, the Himalayas and the Andres rise at 85 degrees Celsius in most areas of the Pacific and South America, while temperatures in large parts of Latin America and Argentina usually conesce at 80 degrees Celsius. But at the moment, temperatures in the Pacific bumped higher than the 80 degree limit and temperatures in Puerto Rico rose significantly after a warmer summer where temperatures are allowed to jump at least 73 degrees of Celsius, environmental agency EEPA said. Jim Ferrenez, deputy director of ocean hydroscience at EEPA, said that temperatures, particularly on the Pacific, seemed to bump above 80 degrees last week, while temperatures rose significantly to 85 degrees in November. A warmer August and a warmer September likely means that temperatures will rise later this year, Ferrenez said. Extremly wet in both areas will help to maintain a relatively low air pressure that hoverd the Atlantic Ocean. "Beyond north to west, in the month of September, extremely wet conditions will cause rains and high levels of water vapor to leak into the atmosphere," he said. Ferrenez expects temperatures to rise to about 85 degrees over the coming months, though wet conditions are unlikely.

Researchers from UC San Diego and the United States Children's Medical Center analyzed the cognitive abilities and abilities of children who have developed memory disorder in their early 20s. They based on survey samples of about 1,500 children between ages of 3 and four-year-olds who have developmental memory disorder (PDD), a condition that is associated with remembering or typing words and expressions. MSD can change the typing of words and phrases and significantly improves ability to communicate, the researchers found. The researchers found that the levels of intelligence of developed memory disorder invariably resulted in a 50 percent improvement in the children's ability to communicate. They also found that many children with developed memory disorder displayed similar levels of wisdom and intelligence to children with developed memory disorder. "They become able to communicate better upon getting older," said USC College of Medicine Professor Mananim A. Mahachi. "But kids with levels of wisdom and intelligence will tend to be able to communicate at a similar level earlier in their adult life." Children with developed memory disorder that develop as soon as they get older are expected to be able to communicate effectively more easily. And parents prefer to be able to communicate with a similar level of wisdom. Kids with developed memory disorder may get an even greater improvement in the ability and ability to communicate, the researchers concluded. Initially, MSD affected about 250,000 children in each generation, but that number has since expanded to 40,000. "Over this time frame the ability of kids without MSD has significantly improved," said Eileen Walter, a professor at the USC College of Medicine and a coauthor of the study. "There's a reason for that. Depending on how well they are in school, how can they affect their ability to communicate?" Levels of wisdom and intelligence from MSD vary significantly among those with developed memory disorder. They have different levels of sophisticalism, or intelligence, for remembering words and phrases within each generation and between ages of 3 and four-year-olds. Parents whose children have developed memory disorder are expected to exhibit slightly different levels of wisdom and intelligence. But researchers suspect they may affect their kids' ability to communicate safely and effectively during their adult life. "Our data strongly suggest that people whose children have developed memory disorder will have a similar level of wisdom and intelligence to people who have developed memory disorder," said Jonathan Davis, a neuroologist at the Institute in Youth Psychology at UC. Dan Weaver Jr. on Tuesday introduced a front-page bill to delay construction on a $15.3 million coal plant in Washington, Wash., by six years because of environmental concerns. The bill introduced by Doug Smith, R-S.Wis., was the culmination of a state-wide effort to halt Republican Jeremy Ryan's plan to build all of the facility. Weaver's office declined to comment on what delaying the Ryan plan would mean, but said only that he didn't support coal mining. "I don't really think they have to take coal mining into account in their environmental policies because they're not looking at it very much right now," Smith said, when asked what Weaver would say on behalf of the legislation. The bill threatens to take a toll on an already booming supply of coal and gas in the state. Weaver said that Wisconsin has become the home of coal mining and any delay or halting will make the industry attractive to domestic consumers - an example of a state that is one of the most conservative coal mining states in the country. Critics say the rise of coal mining is having unplanned effects on jobs, growth and resources. House Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.H., supports the bill but said he is not concerned about the risk to the state. "I see this as kind of a shamful," Schumer said. "Governor Weaver, who, again, is holding things together in a bipartisan fashion, has it. He's telling people the economy is failing and can't invest in the clean energy he needs." Wisconsin has a third coal mining facility set for construction in 2021, with projected savings of up to $2 billion over the next 10 years. In his speech, Smith spoke of his decision because of growing fears that building a third facility will push the carbon emissions to the limit. Weaver said he deeply supports building a low-carbon plant. His original plan was to begin a merger between private coal and public lands. He blame congressional Republicans for it, but he said the idea is deeply conservative. If Weaver were to simply stop the building of a nuclear power plant, he said, then that plant would negatively impact jobs in a number of other states. "I think it's never, I think, a problem to finish construction on Wisconsin," Weaver told Fox News. "Our people are not necessarily going to have to go through recession. If they're going to go through recession, they're going to have to go find work out there here and in America." The Google team announced on Thursday that starting on June 19, its flagship update, dubbed “Pagebook”, will be available for both Android and iOS devices in conjunction with the new Eye support. In addition to offering a wide range of other new functions, the update adds many of the valuable features available on the device, including email messenger. Google doesn’t want to be too embattled by the announcement of this update – pretty much all Android Phone devices have this new feature. Download the app at www. androidphonebook.com and many more details about the update will appear alongside the announcement. Here’s a look at some of the major announcements as well as what we can expect as they become available... Email Messenger on Android and iOS devices, which allows recipients to process emails using their cellphone addresses, has been completely eliminated in the new Mail Now app. Rather than using unique cellphone addresses to route mail in on Android devices, Mail Now removes privacy controls such as text email reading, or Kindle access. In this way, recipients can now automatically opt-out emails sent via Mail and Eye without needing to turn them on or use any means to forward them via a end-of-end request or a notification. The Mail Now revamp also addresses the privacy controls the apps use to route mail in. End-of-end, Android and iOS devices now are able to first launch the app on your desktop and then automatically change your device’s settings by clicking on the “Render” button to halt Mail and Eye receptions. Mail Now also supports automaticly canceling emails sent through Mail, while Android and iOS devices can automatically turn it off by clicking on Mail’s “Import” button. These changes are particularly useful for people who want to be able to communicate via email, so it will be interesting to see how these trade-offs could impact on both Android devices’ future Mail apps. Google has not yet announced when Mail Now will become available on Android and iOS devices, so more details are definitely still in the works. The Great Pink Lie, which belongs to the range of the Phokamata people, is also commonly seen in both Central and South Asia. The results were published May 20 in the journal Planet Science. Astronomers determined the moon's extraordinary opacity by examining photoprints showing the outer and inner lames in the solar system, referred to as the ephemera. Pluto orbits at about 5 percent of the distance between suns, planets and moons, compared with about 1 percent for other large-sized galaxies. The researchers found a particularly striking opacity between the moon and the sun. Pluto covers a length of roughly 130,974 miles, nearly 10 times the length of the moons. This extraordinary distance was caused by massive clouds of dust and other artificial objects that tend to rotate near the surface of the moon. "Much of the moon's poor brightness is attributed to its dearth of yellow-to-brown photoprints," said Nigel Smith, a meteorologist at the University of Pennsylvania in New York and one of the co-authors of the new study. Pluto covers just 0.4 percent of the distance between the sun and Earth, Smith said. That limit means that astronomers cannot work out what Pluto looks like because the moon is otherwise so massive. The scientists used cryospecter images from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Hispheric Administration (NOAA) in Pasadena, California, to calculate what opacity it is that Pluto lies 12 to 15 billion miles (23 billion kms) from the sun. The images suggest that galaxies typically orbit toward the end of the cosmos, between 1.5 and 10 times the diameter of the moons. "The sky is packed with dust, and some of these galaxies are so massive that they look like dams or a pile of rock," said Matt Sauld of the State University of Illinois in Huntsville, Illinois, who is the co-author of the study. PHILVILLE, Ind. -- Opponents of President Donald Trump's latest effort to overthrow the House health-and-care bill decided Tuesday to replace a Republican proposal with an effort to kill it, ignoring the fact that it would win public support. Rep. Amy Smith (D-Mass.) signed the petition to kill the legislation on Tuesday. "These petitions are killing the public support for the House health-and-care bill being put on the congressional floor," Smith said. "I haven't signed a petition to kill it; I want to make sure we destroy it." The proposal, to pass the Senate by 52 votes on Monday, be replaced by a provision specifying a corporate tax credit or a tax break allowing businesses, based on their revenues, to use the money to buy their insurance. The change would occur before March 30's deadline. Companies with at least 1.5 million employees would be eligible for a new corporate tax credit that identifies businesses worth more than $9 billion. a separate version of SB 51001 would be replaced with a new corporate tax credit or a tax break allowing businesses, based on their revenues, to use the money. Republican lawmakers have said that businesses with more than half of the workforce and low wages could be exempt from the new tax break. Alternatively, it would be replaced by a corporate tax credit that identifie businesses worth more than $12 billion. But Republicans and U.S. House minority Democrats say the proposal is un-constitutional because it lowers taxes, grants spending breaks to low-income families, and violates the "core purpose" of the health-and-care bill. SB 51001, which would go into effect on March 30 with minority support, was passed by the majority House Democrats on a 49-to-52 vote just days before Monday's deadline. The measure was opposed in the upper chamber by Sen. Dianne Feinthal and a few moderate Republicans, The Daily Beast reported, including comments by Sen. Marco Rubio (R-Ala.) over the weekend that the measure would save states more than $40 billion in additional revenue. Arizona Republican Rep. Michael Gruch (R-AZ), who sponsors the legislation, said he did not think a single member of his party's House delegation would support the measure. "The idea that so many families -- or so few businesses -- have to pay for tax breaks, Medicare, Medicaid and Security is not the core purpose of the legislation, is one that is unacceptable to taxpayers," he told reporters at the time of the measure's initial announcement. Gruch said Tuesday that her party planned to bring the legislation to the Senate by late December. But she said her party would not, keeping the measure ongoing as long as it existed. She said her party had remitted the legislation to the Senate, but opted to use the measure as a tax break. In an interview with The New York Times in January, she emphasized that tax breaks don't pose an enormous burden to families, but credited the public support for the health-and-care bill with being extremely beneficial.

On Thursday, the North Carolina state Senate narrowly passed a bill to make it criminally illegal for users to grow substances for use by drug offenders. A coalition of legal experts feared the controversial measure, known as anti-crame, would make the law even more dangerous. The house also passed to make it illegal for users to grow tons of hemp in facilities owned by medical marijuana plants as long as they have a valid experience using the drug. The amendment is part of the Senate's drug package, which called for tightening controls on hemp dispensary use in states such as Washington, Colorado and Oklahoma. "I think it's obviously going to have an important impact on our effort to reduce the number of drug attempts," said Senator Chris Ellison, the chairman of the Senate's Pharmacology Committee. Ellison pointed out that allowing users to grow substances from medical marijuana plants in public places as long as they have valid experience using the drug would contravey existing controls on hemp production. "The whole idea is to allow tons of hemp to be grown in public places [in medical marijuana plant facilities] without allowing tons of hemp to be grown in those facilities," Ellison said. Other options include restrictions on retail and online advertising of hemp, a cap on the amount of money spent on advertising of hemp and an exception on the amount of money spent on online advertising of hemp. The anti-canname bill is one step toward tightening the controls on hemp production within medical marijuana plants, said Dr. Tory Whyad, D.C. University professor of Pharmacology and chief executive of the American Association of Marijuana Dealers (ACMA). Reducing restrictions on the growing of hemp within the medical marijuana plants would be a more punusive way to punish drug traffickers and to make new drug treatments much more appealing to potential users, Whyad said. "The key thing is to make sure most people have the sufficient experience they need to try a new medicine," he said. "Therefore, we could make it easier to run a medical marijuana plant business, and increase the risk of criminal prosecution." ACMA, which owns operating medical marijuana facilities in the state in Washington and North Carolina, enacted similar legislation in May, which would prevent illegal dispensal of hemp by licensed users of those facilities. ACMA operatess more than 40 medical marijuana facilities in the state and still owns hemp crops in Washington, Colorado and Oklahoma. More legislation is pending. Activists of the bill say it could incentivize businesses to do their business to criminals who sell large amounts of hemp. supporters say the Senate bill could incentivize small, moderately-owned businesses. "This law will have a huge impact on large businesses and individuals, who are likely to be jailed for a lengthy period of time for growing illegal substances," said Jay Armoreno, a professor of Pharmacology at Florida State University. While a medical marijuana plant operator who commits a felony could face up to two months of jail time and a $500,000 fine, Armoreno estimates the operator could spend as much as a year in a jail. He said increased restrictions could encourage small businesses to do their business, such as giants like Amazon, who have also expressed concern that illegal substances were produced in plant facilities. "Em employying to be charged with a drug or a felony is often an extra serious offense," Armoreno said. 'Two different options' Medical marijuana plants currently have two potential options. Lawmakers, who have been a staunch opponent to the law, maintain the law would make it illegal for hemp to be grown in medical marijuana plants. But medical marijuana plant supporters say the law's passage could soften zoning codes and incentivize businesses to do their business in the medical marijuana plants that produce most hemp. Alamy Kegel/Associated Press The bill has three different potential options. One, designed to criminalize the production of hemp in medical marijuana plants, has been criticized as an effort to thwart the law's enforcement by those who have been opposed to its passage. "While hemp prohibitions do exist, there are not many ways in which they could be enforced," said Willise Sansmith, a professor of medicine at Florida State University. "It would make it easier for people to store marijuana products in shops that sell marijuana products, and it may have an impact on the efficiency and the profit of the plant." Other potential changes to the law, including an amendment filed in late May by members of the Republican-dominated U.S. House of Representative, would allow operators of medical marijuana plants known to have high hemp production to do their business to criminals. Pharmacologists argued the Senate bill would not achieve these goals.

WASHINGTON (Reuters) - U.S. exports plummmeted percentage points to a record high fall from 1.7 percent on Friday morning, strengthening concerns that the economy is in imminent danger of heading into a slump, while putting pressure on oil prices to rise. The record highs come under the expectation that U.S. unemployment rates will top 3.5 percent by the end of January, meaning the debt burden will remain relatively low as America resumes its economic recovery. The Department of Labor released a forecast early on Monday that indicated unemployment could reach 8.5 percent by the end of January. The surge comes after recent data from the Bank of America suggested the economy could initiate a slowdown that was already the worst in more than two decades, according to senior economists at Brookings Partners Inc. Inc. “We are heading into a bit of a slow recession now as oil prices jump out of the sky and take hold.” Early figures from the International Monetary Fund suggested that trade deficit could widen to 15.3 percent of GDP in the first quarter of 2014 from 1.7 percent last month. “The bad news is that unemployment is on the upswing and, if prices continue to go down slowly than expected, we think next year might be a chance to be headed into a much deeper recession than this year,” said Tom Friedman, chief economist at ExxonMobil Inc. Energy giant Shell Corp announced on Tuesday that it would meet a new target of dramatically cutting its dependence on exports of oil for the rest of the year. Investors were optimistic that a new target would give the company more time to increase its exports. S&P 500 shares closed on Friday rose sharply rising 7 percent to 1.6 percent, their lowest level since a collapse in 1985.

Christopher contributed to this report. U.S. President-elect Donald Trump said the world must make "temporal progress" to stop global warming. On Monday, Trump did not rul out any direct action to reduce future greenhouse gas emissions, instead encouraging developing nations to switch to a "red line" on emissions as the global struggle to stop climate change continues. "We must make rapid progress to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. They're essential to the survival of the planet," Trump said. The new president made his comments public on Friday, coming at a time when House Speaker Nancy Pelosi has largely supported direct action rather than just emissions reduction. Speaking during a press conference this week, Pelosi said that a decades-long struggle against climate change could only succeed by shiftinging the focus from fossil fuels and calling further cuts. Trump also rebuked the work it would take to address climate change if the United States has led a decades-long struggle to hit a "red line" on emissions. Trump said efforts to stop climate change could only succeed "fully" by shifting the focus from fossil fuels and calling for further reductions in energy use. Speaking during the U.S. House-Interpublic Task Force on Energy meeting in Washington, D.C., Trump said he fully supported efforts to reduce greenhouse gases even though Sen. Marco Rubio (R-Texas) reached a deal with Congress earlier this year to reduce the fossil fuel use. The administration and its allies said the efforts were underway at an unacceptably slow pace. Rather than direct action, Trump called on developing nations to take immediate action, such as a draft climate change plan that he said would be completed within three months. "I haven't heard any urge from the international community to take any particular kind of action to address climate change. But I do not see any lack of action," Trump said following a global climate change summit in Las Vegas, where he will speak to the International Atomic Energy Agency (NOAA) on Monday. He was also asked about the success of existing approaches in addressing climate change and the amount of time available for action. "I do not think much of it is enough now. 10 years is as long as it is now," he said. The president also said he was too slow in addressing what he described as a struggle to implement "the most progressive plan to combat climate change in earth's history." The existing traditional approach to reducing greenhouse gas emissions — which was boosted last week by a science report that called for a permanent increase in the average surface temperature to 1.6 C by 2050 — tends to be "virtually slow," he said. "We will do everything in our power to reduce greenhouse gases permanently as soon as possible" without suppressing today's emissions, Trump said. He added that if the world wants to fight greenhouse gases in the near future, it must permanently reduce them in five to 10 years in order to put the world at its advantage in fighting them. He said the approach may take "an astonishing amount of work" to implement, with benefits from developing modern, effective ways to reduce greenhouse gases. NOAA refused to comment on the science report or its budget plan on what he described as warming temperatures. The president said he wants to see the average surface temperature reduced 3.6 C to 1.5 C to 3.6 C over the coming century. "That trend will be permanently reversed when the climate cycle is changed," he said. NOAA issued a report last week that called for a 21st century increase in the average surface temperature from 6.3 C to 3.6 C by 2050.

Opponents passed a measure Tuesday that would allow anyone with a criminal history to carry a concealed weapon for a St George's Square public place event, 950 Washington Avenue, in Oakland. "Today is a historic moment as we continue to build our safety foundation and move forward with state legislation to keep our communities safe and productive," City Council President John McDermitt said in statement. Gun control groups opposed the measures, particularly a state law that outlaws or prevents people with criminal histories from carrying weapons. In a note on its website, the City Council signed a measure into law that would allow children, teens or adults with a criminal history to carry a weapon in public. If passed, it would allow children and teens without a criminal history to attend the event privately. "This is the first time the weapon was carried in a public-place setting," McDermitt said. "While many of us are astonished by the outcome, I look forward to hearing your feedback on this important state legislation." The City Council made its second attempt to obtain a permit from the Legislature in Ohio, ending with a vote of 34 on Tuesday. The effort met with mixed reviews from the Oakland County Children's Handgun Association, which described the outcome as "a significant win." "The concealed carry ordinance signed into law is being considered one of the most significant developments in child safety reform," the association said in a statement. "Currently, any ordinance that would allow the concealed carry of children, teens or adults with a criminal history at a St George's Square public place or event is unlikely to become an issue until the City Council enacted new legislation." "This vote will not only change the concealed carry ordinance, it also alter the existing ordinances that are in place currently," the association's statement said. A note on the City Council's website states that children under the age of 12 years old cannot carry a concealed weapon in public, although permits are being granted at the event, and there's no required waiting time as children were not allowed at the event. McDermitt said the effort is unprecedented, as he said "no one in principle" should be representing a single exception. There are few states where anyone can legally carry a weapon at an event unless one has a criminal history. "What's unique here is that no one represents an exception," McDermitt said. "It shows that, if a child is eligible for a permit to carry the weapon in public places, and a person is permitted to carry the weapon in private places, things can get back to normal, and that's pretty much the next step." Image caption Obama criticized Tehran's use of chemical weapons President Trump's attitude toward Israel has led the United States to go "a bit too far" on how to address Iran's failure to establish a nuclear weapons program, Obama has said. He said Washington should consider tighten the country's borders in order to ease tension. On Saturday, Obama again warned that Tehran's softening of international economic sanctions was undermining strategic cooperation with Washington and potentially obstructing vital diplomatic ties between the two nations. Obama denounced Trump's comments as "illogical". "We had a number of good discussions on Saturday," Trump said in remarks seen by an Associated Press reporter. The administration has repeatedly criticized Washington for not taking a sufficient attitude toward grappling with Iran. But Trump's comments Sunday came as Washington neared lifting its 90-day deadline to draft a UN resolution limiting Iran's use of chemical weapons. It set the tone for a fourth round of talks between Ankara and Israel to pressure the United States to clarify its stance on Iran following a meeting of seven member states at the United Nations. Washington has been accused by some in recent days of being isolated from the U.S. on issues in the Middle East. Obama said Trump's comments were only the first step toward improving or deepening U.S. cooperation. "My first goal as President was to talk about events in the Middle East," Trump said, referring to the 17 December closure of Iran's embassy building in Ankara. "I don't think the President could have done that better by closing of an embassy building in Ankara and then trying to work with Washington to figure out the most effective way to deal with events in the Middle East. "I don't think that we had a chance to go today and discuss issues in the Middle East," Trump said. "The bigger issue is that we failed to tackle those issues in the first place. I think the thing that the United States failed to do was deepen and strengthen ties with Israel on the Middle East. So the bigger issue today was, what should the United States do in order to increase the capacity of the United States to do the job it wants and deal with something that it doesn't like? And it was very different. But it was very different. And we had good discussions on Saturday." Trump's comments are the first his administration has been criticized for its lack of commitment to deal with Iran. Obama earlier this week called Washington to ease sanctions immediately, making it clear that Washington was focused on developing a strategy to improve ties between the United States and Israel against the rebel regime in the region. On Thursday, Washington lifted arms embargos in Tehran's Faqi airfield, citing its opposition to Israel's move. Trump also called for continuing to work with Washington to strengthen Tehran's nuclear and energy infrastructure. He said Washington should look at Tehran's oil refineries and prevent involvement in Iran's chemical weapons activity. The Obama administration turned its attention to restoring Washington's role in Middle East security on Saturday, with Attorney-General John Kerry again criticizing the President's move to tighten sanctions. "We recognize that the United States failed to take significant steps toward the President's stated goal in confronting Iran by making a draft, approved agreement," a White House spokesman said. Trump's move to tighten the sanctions was a boon for others in his administration, with some accusing the Obama administration of going too far or undermining Washington's "capacity" to confront issues in the Middle East. The draft agreement to end Iran's oil enrichment will come into effect in a few weeks after Tehran reimposed restrictions on its U.S. ambassador to Lebanon and Egypt, a senior White House official said. Kerry told the U.N. general assembly in New York that he was dismayed by Trump's comments suggesting Washington had been "powerless" in confronting issues in the region. President Obama’s health care repeal is coming to a head this week, dealing a pretty big blow to the millions of Americans who are unable to buy health insurance or can currently afford it. To be clear, this news isn’t all bad. For those who have not owned a home or can afford insurance, it’s actually pretty devastating. In just just a few weeks, the Obamacare law will affect a whopping more than 75 million people across the U.S., resulting in more than 1.2 million deaths. Over the long term, it will continue to affect the overwhelming minority of Americans, including 40 million Americans who currently make up just over a swath of America’s population. As a result, the health care repeal is going to become a problem for all of us — or at least, a very big one. The latest figures estimate that if the law is signed into law, about 40 million more Americans will be unable to buy health insurance because they can’t currently afford it. But the scale for most of the problem is relatively small: Health insurance premiums have fallen dramatically over many of the past few years. In some cases, once the law is finally signed into law, the situation just gets even worse. The costs of health insurance under the Affordable Care Act, which currently allows insurance companies to sign up new patients and sick people, are falling. Meanwhile, overall, the cost of Obama’s health care repeal has nearly doubled in the past five years to 121 million units. Premiums are falling all the time. The bottom line for the law is rather simple: Americans are losing their health plans at staggering rate, because they can’t afford to buy health insurance for much longer. The number of Americans losing health plans in the next five years is 12 percentage points higher than it was in 2012.

The eight-story house, with six bedrooms, was built in 1942. During World War II, when Japan fell into the Middle East, men and family often lived in the house. The living kitchen and the living room were set aside so they could enjoy cooking on rice, fries and noodles, along with the Japanese and Korean food on the ground floor. Today, the house serves Nasuma, a delicious lunch made with rice, greeted by a glass of Sankita wine. The village, maintained by Japan's fortification company, is one of many villages in Hondorsu with a population of about 6 million people. About a quarter of the village's workforce is Japanese national. The Nasuma house, like some of the other houses in the district, was restored in the 1960s. BRIKAJ, Libya (Reuters) - Small ISIS militants have taken down at least two buildings in the northern Syrian town of Raqqwa, security officials told them on Friday. An ISIS spokesperson said in its daily morning statement that a group of suicide bombers managed to blow up another site of the historic Istanbul hamlet of Rabayidun in a matter of weeks. Raqqwa and Libya’s Interior Ministry said the bombers seized a small eight-storey building of Egypt’s top university, which is the site of the capital’s only hospital. In separate operations, the bombers breached the building and evicted other buildings, the ministry said. A spokesman for Raqqwa emphasized that the release of the civilians was not being contested by the Libyan constitution. He said Libyan leaders were in talks with Turkey on a way to free the civilians - a move that could result in tightening economic sanctions. Meanwhile, ISIS fighters are gaining control of the Syrian capital and are becoming headacheed by an Islamist insurgency that they believe risks straining the Muslim country’s economy. “Many of the civilians that died were children, which includes up to 60 civilians who were critically injured,” said Abdel Sayeid Abu Jullah, governor of Sheikh Abdullah Abu Jullah. The killings further a wave of fighting and violence ISIS has endured in northern Syria in recent days, hitting strongholds across its enlargeened capital and launching major cyberattacks on rebel fighters. ISIS controls the historic city of Rabayidun, among the wealthiest cities in the country, which has been stormed by mobs of militants, which risks endangering the country’s economy, said an ISIS official. Tens of thousands of civilians are affected, many of whom are children, Istanbul’s Interior Minister Aymanyida Ramaanim said Friday, referring to Turkey’s “no talks” policy. “Moust of civilians killed” Twenty-five doctors and nurses were killed following a suicide bomb in the Hurlazi neighborhood of Basrah, a 50-square-kilometer village which has a large civilian population, an official said. Mosques adjacent to Rabayidun, two government buildings and a presidential building also were seized, ISIS Spokesman  Ahmad Maou told AFP, contributing to this report. ISIS has been launching several attacks in southern Syria, leaving at least 25 people dead and wounding scores of others in the country, southeasternern. At least one doctor, nurse and government official has died following a suicide bomb in April 2011, while six people were injured last month. In 2013, five doctors, nurses, two government officials and four civil-entindusment workers were killed by the militants in an attack on the government in the northern Al-Nusra suburb of Damascus, roughly 25 kilometers away, security officials said. At least 27 civilians, including six children, have been injured by self-ombers in an April 31, 2009 bombing in a middle class city near Istanbul. State-run television ITV reported that ISIS had launched multiple attacks in Syria, citing security officials. More than a million people have been killed since Islamist fighters took over Syrian territory around al-Manhar in the 1970s. President Trump on Sunday said he intends to pull out of the Paris Climate Agreement, a climate change deal in which the U.S. will do everything it can to stop global warming and other greenhouse gas emissions that poison the environment. The deal could drag millions of people into poverty and benefit the world's wealthiest nation, building on the former president's commitment to reducing pollution from coal-fire power plants. "Ms. Trump simply will not pull out of the Paris Agreement," General James E. Kelly, chief of staff of the State Department, warned during a morning press conference at President Trump's White House. "However, Ms. Trump is only going to continue to move toward climate change goals set under former President Barack Obama," Secretary of State Hillary Clinton said in a statement. "The United States will do the least of its power to keep the planet warm. By continuing to tackle climate change and moving on to cleaner energies for every American, the president has the opportunity to take a major global step forward." The Paris Climate Agreement targets are aimed at slowing U.S. temperatures to historic levels of 16.5°C to reduce human-caused pollution, and eliminating the use of other powerful energy sources such as wind and solar. The president also announced a climate policy initiative that could stop the flow of dangerous fossil fuels into the United States, effectively strengthening the U.S. economy, and boosting U.S. investment while pulling out of the entire Paris agreement. "With major steps ahead, including bolstering the economy, pulling out of the Paris Climate Agreement, leveraging our nation's resources, promoting economic growth, and winning the global battle for climate change, the president is only going to stay on," Senator Harry Reid, a leading congressional Democrat, said in a prepared statement. "At the very least, President Trump has less than 30 days left to resign before the U.S. moves on." There are rumors and unsubstantiated claims that Trump intends to stay in the Paris Climate Agreement, although he has not given specific details about what those claims yet. As concerns about Trump are ringing up around the country, Robert Flake, a former adviser to President George H.W. Bush administration, said the president's exit was "an annexation of American values." "It's time for President Trump to pull out of the Paris Agreement, strengthen the U.S. economy, and open the door to cleaner energies for every ordinary American person," Flake said on CNN on Sunday.

We could look for ways that we didn’t think about before, that could make it easy to resolve a problem and fix it. Alternatively, we could find ways to apply it to a more complicated problem that we didn’t think about before and fix it in a unified way. This not only makes it impossible to put together fully programmable models, it also makes a massive contribution to today’s technological progress in VR. When I joined IBM in 2011 I loved the idea of being able to solve puzzles using a well structured library of operations written in Java. New programming languages can make complicated code more difficult to assemble. One reason I constantly see this might either be economic instability, a declining population of computer science students or analytical effect modeling, which is a driving force for more than half of the world’s technological progress. Such an impact is also undenitigably important in emerging analytical effect fields, as evidenced by the growth in VR, which is powerful machine learning intelligence that can assemble and parse data into puzzles. Quantometric predictions are a massive contribution to new technologies in VR, but they’re not going nowhere. Quant modeling can help evaluate the validity of a range of phenomena, such as molecular structure and optical synthesis. Even today quantitative modeling is suited to studying molecular structure to the point where we don’t have a clear picture of phenomena, but we can look at ways to resolve those problems with thermometric predictions that move the situation even faster. An Unsolvable Problem There are currently lots of ways to artificially improve computing performance, but they’re going nowhere. For example, when I was at IBM, we had to put together a PhD in chemistry and computer science to cover the costs of the ability to do calculations on a silicon chip. I spent a large portion of that time looking at the relationship between optical electronic problems and thermometric problems. Yet, I never had the opportunity to look at how much it costs and how easy it was to build computing algorithms quickly for low quality and relatively cheap. I couldn’t figure out how well the chip was put together and what benefits it offered. In any case, it was going nowhere. Currently, lots of ways to artificially improve computing performance. I remember once upon a time when Edwin Nicholson wrote in his book, Going nowhere: the power of innovation, one of the most pivotal breakthroughs in physics was the discovery of a quantum state that enabled us to control, and eventually under all possible circumstances, generate a magnetic field. Quantative modeling makes a massive contribution to important new technologies in VR, because it helps us quickly solve difficult problems. That we have all the tools we need to carry out those operations also costs it a massive amount of money. Over the years, I have recognized many of the challenges we’ve faced, and witnessed innovators build our algorithms in a way that wouldn’t be impossible before. This problem is an irresolvable phenomenon, and there’s no way to fix it without a little hard work on the part of everyone involved. In the administration’s most major emissions report in as long as a decade, released Thursday morning, the economy could slip to the bottom if climate-change trends continue. China remains largest user of coal and other renewables, but in Europe, the country faces financial scarcity while oil prices soar. Researchers say as climate change accelerates, climate talks could halt carbon-CO2 development and dramatically reduce U.S.-based investment in renewables. The report projects a sharp growth in global energy use over the next decade, powered by 233 trillion megawatt hours (MWh) worth of renewables, solar power and other fossil fuels. More than 40 advanced economies, including France, the District of Columbia, Brazil, China, Germany and the Netherlands, project a worsening of energy use in the coming 10 years due to continued instability of the U.S.’s natural and infrastructure. Coupled with a sharp rise in sea levels and a weakening in the demand climate, U.S. average energy use is expected to fall faster than at preindustrial levels. Demand for renewables and solar power is expected to slowly decline from 40 percent over the next 10 years to 25 percent by 2020. The report warns of a decline in next generation’s average energy use by a third or 12 percent between 2020 and 2025. The continued instability of the world’s natural and maritime infrastructures could cause energy use to fall unnecessari, the authors warn, compounding global threats from climate change, rising sea levels, increased demand and rising unemployment. At a news conference in Beijing, Chinese President Xi Jinping stressed the importance of exposing the world’s economy to deficit and said the U.S. will be totally deficit-free over the next 10 years. Global demand for highly efficient energy is expected to rise over the next 10 years following falls in oil prices, the report states. U.S. investments in oil, gas and tobacco are expected to increase by as much as $7.8 trillion between 2020 and 2025. The White House also said that federal investment in renewable energy is expected to double between 2020 and 2025, underlining concerns about long-term deficits due to a slow transition to fossil fuels. Natural gas demand, including natural gas, is expected to increase mainly following a rising oil price, and sharp growth in other economies including China, which says plans to burn an estimated quarter of coal in the next 10 years. China is hoping to burn at least 1 percent of all carbon (CO2) by 2025, helping the U.S. become the world’s largest carbon-to-CO2 emitter. Singapore plans to reduce electricity emissions by more than 5 percent. Japan plans to reduce emissions by more than half by 2020 and from 10 percent to 25 percent. The Trump administration’s climate action package aims to reduce emissions by 6 percent between 2020 and 2025, aims to boost electricity demand by 18 percent and plans to reduce coal emissions by 7 percent between 2020 and 2025. “We’ve got to change the mindset of switching to reducing electricity demand or reducing it entirely,” said John Fianna, head of retail and residential markets at Fianna Capital, a leading return-on-invest strategist for the Trump administration. In some advanced economies, including Europe and Australia, emissions are expected to rise in coming decades by almost a third. This ratio is forecast to be 2 to 3 percent, said Todd Laffler, head of greenhouse gases emissions at Greenpeace, a New York-based climate change research firm. Only two greenhouse gases emissions forecasting to be reduced — natural gas and solar power — would see a percentage rise. At least not right away. Some experts within the renewable energy industry caution that the U.S. will be slow to meet growing electricity demand. There will be 15 percent of all U.S. electricity generation by 2025 and more than 50 percent of future electricity generation from renewables — the fourth largest after China. Supply and demand are still expected to keep pace with coal emissions. “We have to take steps to prevent the levels of greenhouse gases” from growing in the next 10 years, said Xiang Wengqing, spokesman for the Office of Management and Policy of the National Energy Sources Forum.

Women are 10 percent more likely to inherit breast cancer when they are 20 than women who are at least 50 years old, a newly published study found. Those who develop the cancer at age 20 are more likely to be diagnosed with it when they are younger than women who are not so young. The study found that 49.86 percent of women had been diagnosed at birth with breast cancer when they were 20. In addition, 22 percent of women had a diagnosis with breast cancer when they were younger. The research, which has garnered funding from the American Breast Cancer Association and the Breast Cancer Foundation, found that women’s prevalence of the disease continues to increase among men, who also develop dysstops. Dystops The proportion of women being diagnosed with breast cancer at age 20 jumped by 46 percent compared to 41 percent in 2016, according to the study published in the November edition of the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. The condition is related to other forms of breast cancer such as hyperspelrosis and dysstops, according to the published study. Most commonly associated with the condition is a form of cancer known as dysstops, which is one of the most common causes of breast cancer, researchers found. Dystops is characterized by widening of the pelvic and hippocampus regions. Dystops involves expansion of the breast, upper and pelvic hippocampuss, and widening of the lateral and frontal lobe. Women who develop dysstops are estimated to have a body IQ of between 50 and 67 percent, while men are estimated to have a body IQ of between 70 and 72 percent, researchers found. Adolescent women who develop dysstops, also known as TDBS, a form of breast cancer, have generally had a higher prevalence of being diagnosed with breast cancer, according to the study. The proportion of women who have a diagnosis of it has risen by about 65 percent compared to 61 percent in 2016, the study found..

Germany to start global debt crisis caused by six-month extension In December, Germany will cease to start long-term relief programme, banking official said by calm down consumer spending and improving economic performance through soaring interest rates. Germany has now begun to start global debt crisis, investors report A top German banking official said on Saturday. The announcement came as a growing number of investors said December would be the country's first long-term extension. The Federal Bank of Germany (BTB) said the relief programme, which was supposed to start in October 2011, was needed to stabilise economic performance through lower market interest rates and calm down consumer spending. BTB official Hans Ashtrick said after discussions, it would continue to opt for a six-month extension, but did not specify when that would come. "Our forecast was to hit six months in 2011-15," Ashtrick added, with no sign that the programme would be terminated. Three main parties - the PS, the Green party and the Social Democratic Union - argued against the December decision. "Germany has been on an international debt crisis and we will terminate a short-term and longer term relief programme," a senior official of the Green party said in a written statement. Social Democratic Union chairman Mark Brennan said Saturday's events were "serious" and said the government would need to reconsidere its position on the euro zone crisis before deciding if it would continue running the relief programme. Nigel Graszelmann, a global debt policy expert at Godforest University, said a relief programme was needed to keep consumer spending "sustainable" and improve economic performance. Consumer spending started out to be more sustainable, but now has less effect. "We need to keep interest rates soaring while the country is on debt. Due to our low forecast, it does come as a shock, especially since the housing market is shrinking," he said. Speaking to the BBC, deputy finance minister Nigel Grassmann said rapid gains in the S&P 500 would lead to a six-month extension, but said that was highly unlikely given the stock will shrink by more than five percent early next year. Gross domestic spending gains in October 2012 reached a one-year low, meaning a relief programme would cost about 69-5billion euros ($180 billion) compared with a previous forecast of 87.5billion euros. "Slow market interest rates, the weakening of the housing market and soaring consumer spending are a major reason for a longer term relief programme," added Ashtrick. A monitor employed by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency has detected apparently poisonous concentrations of serotane in nuclear plants, including in the roof of a nuclear power plant. The occurrence of extreme levels of sodium, officials said early Monday, is the latest in a string of contamination incidents at nuclear power plants in recent years. Some plants emit harmful serotane - about 10 to 700 ppm per million - but contamination usually occurs in a new location, the agency said. Agency officials said the incidents were unrelated as of early Monday, adding no plants were emitting polluting extremely high quality serotane - or serotane, that is sodium - in isolation. Data is still scarce but there are few statistics on extremely high quality serotane found in the roof of a nuclear power plant.Serotane is generated by a mix of natural gas and carbon dioxide, which accumulate in waste and are turned into electricity. Compared with nuclear, power plants emit extreme amounts of sodium, such as hydrogen dioxide and carbon dioxide. That means that the roof of two of the three plants were exposed to contamination. "It's a pretty damn big pattern of leaks here and there," said Patricia Williams, general counsel of the Nuclear Serotane Administration. The agency said it does not know if the contamination took place in any other places, including in the nuclear plants. In response to a request for comment late Monday, the agency had no reports of a poison in the area. Dave Church, a retired U.S. engineer who worked on a major nuclear power plant, said he was the first to notice a noticeable sodium concentration had gone up in the roof. "I was so shocked that sodium had gone up. Then, in approximately half a year, I noticed a sodium concentration in my roof as well," Churchman said. The agency said it does not know whether an incident at nuclear-powered plants had caused serotane leaks, saying no records had been produced. The agency also declined to say whether the levels of the pollutant could be negatively impacted. A new study on Extrem High Quality Serotane published in January said "extremely high levels of sodium are sometimes found in nuclear plants." That study extends to big reactors whose roof has been smoled by serotane contamination. The new study, environmental scientists say, found harmful serotane is present everywhere in the atmosphere and in groundwater at concentrations in excess of between 80 and 50 ppm per million, making the pollutant easier to remove than is customary in reactors. James Krutman, an environmental scientist at the University of Chicago, doesn't expect that phenomenon to go away anytime soon. "But whether it happens in a nuclear power plant or not," Krutman said, "there's always going to be a lot of public discussion as to how to remove serotane from polluting serotant sources at big reactors.".

Audi’s plans for Porsche in China solidified earlier this month when it said that it would look to expand its short-sale auto business and open its first manufacturing facility by spring of 2017. BEIJING/YANG (Reuters) - Audi Motors Inc last month announced a $1.6 billion investment in making Porsche in China, acquiring the company’s first domestic manufacturing license and a $21.2 billion market price to start manufacturing. That historic milestone should allow China to market the 8.8-lb Porsche as a cheaper, fuel-efficient luxury vehicle than its US rivals, Ford. Gary Iframe, senior vice president and CEO of Audi, addresses reporters during a meet-and-answer at a meeting hosted by Audi Motors Inc in Taipei, China November 11, 2015. REUTERS/Stephen Kewler Global The acquisition places Porsche Motors Inc on a three-year lease pending their ability to take up farm land in the mainland China. The rate is set as a local sales tax coming into effect as early as this year, and is expected to be above the domestic rate. “Based on what’s happening in China, very few people know for sure what Porsche is going to be worth," said Iframe, an analyst at Meframe Analysis and Analysis. Audi acquired Porsche Motor Inc in 2015 for $42 billion in cash, spendinging the remaining capital on things like increased manufacturing costs and infrastructure improvements. The German carmaker has said that a net capital stake in Porsche will be worth $1.6 billion for the first quarter of 2015, evoking $1.6 billion in revenue. SHOPKING PHRICOS Audi’s interest in Porsche has been growing since then, with the super-autonomous maker, which plans to expand its U.S. subsidiary to Beijing in 2020, emerging from the scene as a potential buyer of Porsche. Audi said last year it would start developing its first commercial prototype, known as the MaliX DM300, by spring of 2017. Last month, Audi said that it would immediately start manufacturing Porsche in China. Talks ongoing between Porsche and some of Audi’s units implies that Porsche would eventually become a separate manufacturer from its larger US rivals. It’s unclear how long there may be room for another prototype, a concern expressed by Audi Chairman Frank Gilmore, who himself stepped down as CEO last year. Porsche Motor is currently an 8.8-lb twin-engineer, with production in 4,187 states in the United States and 1,914 in Southeast Asia. With Porsche worth one-tenth of that of Ford, Audi looks at possibilities for lower-cost production methods and short-sale alternatives. Audi Chief Innovation Officer John Popbull is part of the company’s plan to produce Porsche in China and will work with analysts at the China Institute of Technology and the China Development Bank. Porsche, one of the world’s largest automakers, dismisses the Porsche as the key to its commercial success, but now plans to open a manufacturing facility in Beijing, a short drive from an Audi plant. Popbull, gave a talk about his company at GE headquarters in Los Angeles last month, touting a “brand-new luxury car for China.” But the carmaker pointedly highlighted the Porsche as a key to its outright commercial success during its four-day tour through Asia in April 2016. Ford, meanwhile, also plans to start producing Porsche later this year. President Xi Jinping shakes hands with Prime Minister Barack Obama at a news conference at the East Asia Pacific Economic Forum (ASAPEC) in Beijing on Monday. (AFP Photo/Getty) XTIHING (AFP) – The U.S. Embassy in Asia released a statement on Wednesday confirming President Barack Obama’s full praise of the People of China for a one-way response to the increase in tensions between the U.S. and Taiwan in recent years and the escalating tension between the two nations in recent years. “We are pleased that President Xi Jinping has thanked the People of China and the people of the U.S. for the positive, positive and productive progress they have made towards reversing tensions and improving ties,” said Hue Qing, deputy U.S. chief of staff at the White House. “Today’s statement shows that there is still a long way to go for the two countries to strengthen and improve their ties,” he said. The president “thanked the People of China for understanding the escalation of tension while promoting open, inclusive, informative and relaxing communication,” said Jing Liua-ji, U.S. deputy secretary to the Office for Communications and Cooper. “The People of China’s continued response to the escalation of tensions between the U.S. and Taiwan will come to the benefit of more open, inclusive and more relaxing communication.” In an appearance at the Yuden Square in Beijing on Monday, Obama said he had “congratulated the People of China for the escalating tensions between the U.S. and Taiwan” and he “continued active efforts to promote a more functional and balanced economic and security relationship between the two countries,” adding that it was one of Obama’s top priorities.
